ce-6.validate: Formulate AI-use rules for your class. Discuss them with students — their reaction will show what you missed.

claude-for-educators.trigger: You're preparing materials, feedback, and personalization — and time is always tight.
outputs: Lesson plan + level-adapted variants
Feedback and grading templates
Personalized assignment workflow
claude-for-educators.savings: ~5-8 prep hours/week + better feedback to students

workflow-automation.title: Building an AI Workflow
workflow-automation.subtitle: Projects + Skills + Scenarios into a single automated process
workflow-automation.whatItIs: A practical course on creating AI workflows without code — for any user who wants to turn scattered Claude interactions into a coherent system. You will learn how Projects serve as containers, Skills as reusable modules, and Scenarios as application patterns. By the end you will have built your first end-to-end workflow and documented it for your team.
workflow-automation.approach: The course is structured as a workshop: each step produces an artifact you create for a real task from your own work. Theory is minimal — every concept is immediately reinforced with practice. By the final step you will have a documented workflow ready to hand off to a colleague.
outcomes: Can analyse a task and extract the workflow pattern: input → process → output
Structure Projects as workspaces with persistent context
Write reusable Skills — modules for repeating operations
Build step chains where the output of one step becomes the input of the next
Validate intermediate results — do not rely on Claude blindly
Document a workflow so a colleague can run it without your explanations

applyIn.title: Analytics and reporting
applyIn.description: Turn the cycle 'gather data → analyse → write report' into a repeatable workflow. Every step is documented, quality is stable, the next report takes half the time.

applyIn.title: Content and communications
applyIn.description: Email series, multi-channel posts, regular briefings — a workflow lets you reuse voice and structure instead of reinventing them every time.

applyIn.title: Operational processes
applyIn.description: Onboarding, request processing, meeting prep — any repeatable process with AI can be documented as a workflow and handed to the team without quality loss.

pitfalls: Trying to automate the entire process at once — start with one concrete step, make sure it works reliably, then add the next.
Building a workflow for a task that changes every time — automation adds value only where there is enough repetition and a predictable input.
Skipping validate steps to save time — checking intermediate results takes 2 minutes and prevents cascading errors across the whole chain.

exercises.question: Take any repeating task from your week and map it as a chain: what is the input, what are the transformation steps, what is the final output. How many steps require Claude, and how many require your own judgement?
exercises.hint: Steps that require judgement are your checkpoints. That is exactly where the workflow should pause and wait for human review.

exercises.question: Write a SKILL.md for one repeating operation you do every week. Show it to a colleague and ask: could they run this skill without your help?
exercises.hint: If your colleague asks more than two questions, the skill is not described well enough. Add examples and clarify the input format.

wa-1.title: What is an AI workflow: Projects, Skills, Scenarios
wa-1.why: Without shared terminology it is easy to confuse Projects, Skills and Scenarios — and build chaotic interactions instead of a system.
instructions: An AI workflow is a sequence of steps where Claude does part of the work and a human reviews the result and passes control forward. It is not magic — it is a repeatable process with clear inputs and outputs.
Project — container and workspace. It holds instructions (what Claude knows by default), a knowledge base (documents and context) and interaction history. One Project = one work area or task.
Skill — a reusable module: a description of one specific operation with an instruction, input format, output format and example. A Skill can be run again and again — the result will be predictable.

Scenario — an application pattern: a description of a specific situation where the workflow is used. One Skill can be used in multiple Scenarios. For example, the 'summarisation' skill is used in the 'weekly briefing' scenario and the 'meeting preparation' scenario.
Mental model: Project = the office. Skills = work instructions on the desk. Scenarios = the specific tasks the employee solves every day using those instructions.
wa-1.tip: Do not try to formalise everything at once. Start by describing what you do now — then break it down into Projects, Skills and Scenarios.
wa-1.validate: You can name one task from your work and explain what its Project will be, which Skill is needed and in which Scenario it is executed.

wa-2.title: Anatomy of a good workflow: input → process → output
wa-2.why: A workflow without a clear input/output structure cannot be repeated, handed to a colleague or improved — it runs differently every time.
instructions: Let us break it down with an example: 'preparing an analytical report'. Input: raw data (table, export, set of facts) + the question the report must answer. Process: 3 Claude steps (structure → analyse → format). Output: a finished report draft in an agreed format.
Three questions for any workflow: (1) What must be provided to Claude for it to begin? (2) What steps must be taken and in what order? (3) What does a result that counts as 'done' look like?
Describing the input is the most important part. Undefined input = unpredictable result. A good input description covers: data format, volume, required fields, language and any constraints.
Intermediate outputs are the inputs for the next steps. For each step write down: what is being passed forward and in what format. This lets you find bottlenecks before you run anything.
The final output must have a completion criterion: not 'a good report', but 'a report with an executive summary of up to 200 words, 3–5 key findings and recommendations as bullet points'.
wa-2.tip: Write the workflow on paper before opening Claude. Two hours on a diagram saves eight hours of iteration.
wa-2.validate: For your chosen task you have a description of the input, a list of steps and a completion criterion for the final output.

wa-3.title: Skills: creating your first reusable module
wa-3.why: Without a formalised Skill you reformulate the same task every time — wasting time and getting inconsistent results.
instructions: A Skill is a document with a fixed structure. Minimum contents: name (what the skill does), input (what must be provided), instruction (step-by-step direction to Claude), output (what Claude will return and in what format), example (a concrete input/output pair).
Choose a repeating operation from your work: summarising feedback, preparing a meeting agenda, analysing a competitor, a first-draft email. The more specific the better.

Write the SKILL.md: start with the name and one phrase explaining why this skill is needed. Then an Input section with a concrete example. Then Instructions — what Claude should do, step by step. Then Output — the exact result format. Finally, an example.
Test the skill: open Claude, paste the skill instruction as the system context, provide a test input and evaluate the output. Does it match the described format?
Iterate the skill until the output is stable across three different test inputs. Only then is the skill ready for use in a workflow.
wa-3.tip: The best first skill is one you already do manually every week. Do not invent new tasks to automate — formalise existing ones.
wa-3.validate: You have a finished SKILL.md that you have tested on at least two real inputs and received a predictable output.

wa-4.title: Chains: output of one step becomes input of the next
wa-4.why: Connecting steps into a chain is what turns a set of separate Claude interactions into a real workflow.
instructions: Chain principle: the final output of step N exactly matches the described input format of step N+1. If the formats do not match, a transformation step is needed between them.

Practice: take two skills you want to connect. Write down the output format of the first and the input format of the second. Is there a gap? Usually there is — the output is too verbose, or structured differently.

Three ways to close the gap: (1) add an explicit output format to the first skill's instruction that suits the next step, (2) create an intermediate transformer skill that converts the format, (3) add a human step — you manually edit the handoff.
Document the chain: draw a diagram where each block is one step, arrows show data transfer, and diamonds mark human review points. This diagram becomes the workflow documentation.
Test the entire chain end-to-end, not just individual steps. Errors most often appear at the seams between steps, not inside them.
wa-4.tip: Use explicit separators in prompts: 'Here is the output from the previous step: [DATA]. Now perform...'. Explicit context passing is more reliable than implicit.
wa-4.validate: You have connected at least two steps into a chain and run real data through it. The output of the second step matches the expected format.

wa-5.title: Quality control: human-in-the-loop and validate blocks
wa-5.why: Claude can make mistakes, hallucinate and interpret ambiguously — blind trust in output in a multi-step workflow leads to cascading errors.
instructions: Human-in-the-loop means points in the workflow where a human checks the result before passing it forward. You do not need to check every step — identify critical points where an error has the greatest consequences.

A validate block is an explicit criterion you check: 'the output contains exactly 5 items', 'all company names match the source data', 'the tone is formal, no jargon'. Write validate blocks for each step where this matters.

Three levels of control: (1) automatic — Claude checks against a checklist built into the instruction, (2) quick scan — 30 seconds, you look at structure and key data, (3) deep review — you read fully and compare with the source.
Red flags requiring deep review: specific numbers and statistics, names and titles, legal and financial language, quotes attributed to specific people.

Add a validate block directly to the skill instruction: 'At the end of your response add a checklist where you mark compliance with each of these criteria: [list]. If a criterion is not met, explain why'.
wa-5.tip: The best validate block is specific and binary: met / not met. 'The text sounds professional' is a bad criterion. 'Does not contain words from this list' is a good one.
wa-5.validate: Every step of your workflow has at least one explicit validate criterion and you know who (human or Claude) checks it.

wa-6.title: Scaling: document and hand off the workflow to your team
wa-6.why: A workflow that lives only in one person's head is not a scalable process — it is a personal habit. Documentation turns it into a team standard.
instructions: Workflow documentation structure: (1) name and purpose in one phrase, (2) when to use it — the trigger, (3) what to prepare — input data, (4) steps with links to Skills, (5) what a good result looks like, (6) common mistakes and how to avoid them.
Validate the documentation: ask a colleague who has never seen this workflow to read the document and try to run it independently. Where they get stuck — those are the gaps.
Versioning: add a 'last updated' date and a brief changelog. Workflows change — the team needs to know which version is current.
Storage: a Claude Project with instructions is ideal for storing workflow documents. All team members have access and the context is always current.
Improvement cycle: after every 10 workflow runs, hold a 15-minute retrospective. What worked? What took extra time? What gave unexpected results? Update the documentation.
wa-6.tip: Good workflow documentation is not a user manual — it is a work instruction. Write it as if you are explaining to a smart new employee who has never done this task.
wa-6.validate: You have a workflow document that another person can use without your verbal explanations. You have verified this in practice.

workflow-automation.trigger: A 3+ step routine repeats ≥3 times per week and eats your focus time.
inputs: Description of the current manual process
outputs: A workflow map: trigger → steps → outcome
A ready prompt + Project for the task
A before/after metric for the team report

role-use-cases.title: Claude by profession
role-use-cases.subtitle: Concrete applications for Marketing, Sales, HR, Product, Customer Success
role-use-cases.whatItIs: A practical course for specialists who already know the basics of working with Claude and want to apply them to tasks specific to their role. Covers five functions: Marketing, Sales, HR, Product, Customer Success — with concrete prompts, templates and workflows for each. In the final step you build your own role playbook.
role-use-cases.approach: Each step focuses on one role and contains specific scenarios, prompts to copy and common mistakes. Even if you work in one function — scan all steps: many patterns transfer between roles. The last step assembles your personal playbook.
outcomes: Apply Claude to 5+ concrete tasks of your role with predictable quality
Created role-specific prompts and templates for your top tasks
Build workflows with Projects for repeating operations in your function
Adapt patterns from adjacent roles to your own tasks
Avoid typical AI mistakes in a corporate context
Documented and ready to share templates with your team

applyIn.title: Marketing and communications
applyIn.description: A content machine with a consistent brand voice: long-form articles, SEO content, email campaigns and posts for multiple channels — Claude adapts one piece of content to all formats.

applyIn.title: Sales and Customer Success
applyIn.description: Personalised outreach, negotiation prep, objection analysis, response templates — Claude helps scale quality without losing personalisation.

applyIn.title: HR and operations management
applyIn.description: From writing JDs to onboarding packages and policies: Claude cuts time spent on administrative documents and helps maintain a consistent tone and standards.

pitfalls: Using one universal prompt for all tasks in the role — every scenario requires its own context and format. Create a separate template for each repeating task.
Publishing Claude-generated content without checking for brand alignment and factual accuracy — especially critical for external communications in sales and marketing.
Ignoring data confidentiality when working with customer or candidate information — use anonymised descriptions and do not input personal data unnecessarily.

exercises.question: Choose the three most time-consuming tasks in your role. Write a prompt for each and test it on a real example. Which of the three gave the best result on the first attempt?
exercises.hint: Tasks with a clear template and standard output format work best with Claude on the first try. Tasks requiring nuance and context improve after a few iterations.

exercises.question: Find a colleague from a different function (Marketing → Sales, HR → Product) and show them your best prompt. Ask them to adapt it to their role. What changed? What stayed the same?
exercises.hint: Prompt structure is usually transferable. Role context and output format change. This will show you what is the essence of the prompt and what is the role-specific layer.

ruc-1.title: Marketing: a content machine with a consistent voice
ruc-1.why: Marketing produces more content than any other function — but every piece must sound the same. Claude solves both challenges simultaneously.
instructions: Brand voice in the [[node:b-system|system prompt]]: add a brand voice description to the [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] — 3–5 adjectives, examples of sentences that sound 'right' and examples that sound 'wrong'. Claude will apply this automatically.

Long-form and SEO: a prompt for an article = topic + target audience + the main question the reader has + keywords + desired length + structure (H2/H3). Ask Claude to write the outline first and approve it before generating the full text.
Email campaigns: use one message as the base — ask Claude to create 3–5 variations of different length and tone (formal / conversational / urgent). A/B testing will show what works best.

Channel adaptation: one piece of content → five formats. Prompt: 'Here is the long-form text: [TEXT]. Adapt it for: (1) LinkedIn post 150 words, (2) Twitter/X thread of 5 tweets, (3) email subject line + preview text, (4) short summary for a newsletter, (5) script for a 60-second video'.
Typical marketer mistake: asking Claude to 'write content' without audience context. Always specify: who the reader is, what they already know, and how they should feel after reading.
ruc-1.tip: Create one reference piece in the Project that perfectly reflects the brand voice. Use it as a reference: 'Write in the same style as this example: [reference]'.
ruc-1.validate: You have created at least one prompt for a specific marketing task and received a result that can be used as a draft without major edits.

ruc-2.title: Sales: from lead to deal
ruc-2.why: Sales requires personalisation at scale — every message must feel hand-crafted, but doing it manually for 50 leads is impossible.
instructions: Personalised outreach: prompt = company profile (industry, size, recent events) + contact profile (role, pain points of the role) + your product + goal of the message (first contact / follow-up / re-engagement). Result: a draft message that only needs to be checked and personalised in 2–3 places.

Objection analysis: create an 'Objection Analysis' skill. Input: the customer's objection as stated. Output: (1) the real concern behind the objection, (2) 2–3 ways to respond, (3) a question that helps understand the depth of the issue.

Negotiation prep: prompt = company name + known deal information + your position + meeting goal. Ask Claude for: likely questions the customer will ask, likely objections, key arguments for your position, red lines that must not be crossed.

After the meeting: 'Here are my notes from the meeting: [NOTES]. Write a follow-up email with: (1) a thank-you, (2) a brief summary of agreements, (3) next steps with deadlines, (4) an open question to keep the dialogue going'.
Important: always verify factual data about the company and customer that Claude includes in messages — hallucinations in sales are especially dangerous.
ruc-2.tip: The best use of Claude in sales is not replacing personalisation but accelerating it. A draft in 30 seconds, personalisation in 2 minutes — instead of writing from scratch in 15 minutes.
ruc-2.validate: You have a template prompt for outreach that you have tested on 3 real leads and received drafts requiring minimal editing.

ruc-3.title: HR: from JD to onboarding
ruc-3.why: HR creates a large volume of repeating documents — and often spends time on them that could be spent working with people.
instructions: Job Descriptions: prompt = role title + key responsibilities (5–7 items) + must-have requirements + nice-to-have + team context + company format. Ask Claude to write a JD that: (1) sounds attractive to the target audience, (2) uses inclusive language, (3) avoids excessive requirements that exclude good candidates.

Structured interviews: 'I am hiring for [ROLE]. Here are 3 key competencies: [LIST]. For each competency create 2 behavioural questions (STAR format) and scoring criteria: excellent / good / insufficient'.

Welcome package for new employees: use a template prompt with variables — employee name, role, team, start date, manager. Claude generates a personalised welcome letter and first-week checklist in 2 minutes.

Policies and guidelines: 'Here is our existing [TOPIC] policy written 3 years ago: [TEXT]. Update it to current standards, make the language clearer, keep the substance. Mark where you made significant changes'.
Confidentiality: never input real candidate or employee names into Claude without their consent. Use initials or role descriptions instead of personal data.
ruc-3.tip: Create a library of template prompts for each HR document type in the Claude Project. One setup session saves several hours every week.
ruc-3.validate: You have written a JD or interview questions with Claude and compared the result to a previous version written manually. Which took less time and was the quality comparable?

ruc-4.title: Product: from Discovery to Spec
ruc-4.why: A Product Manager spends up to 40% of their time writing documents — PRDs, user stories, roadmap justifications. Claude does not replace product thinking but dramatically accelerates turning it into documents.
instructions: User Stories: 'Here are raw notes from user interviews: [NOTES]. Extract 5–7 user stories in the format: As a [role], I want to [action] so that [outcome]. For each add acceptance criteria and a priority (High/Medium/Low) with justification'.

Interview synthesis: 'Here are transcripts from 5 user interviews: [TRANSCRIPTS]. Extract: (1) recurring pain points (with mention frequency), (2) unexpected insights, (3) contradictions across interviews, (4) open questions requiring further research'.

PRD first draft: create a 'First PRD Draft' skill. Input: problem + target audience + proposed solution + constraints. Output: a PRD structure with completed sections and explicit placeholders where data that Claude does not have is needed.

Roadmap justification: 'I am proposing to prioritise [FEATURE] next quarter. Here is the context: [DATA]. Help write a justification for stakeholders including: business case, alternatives we considered, risks and how we mitigate them, success metrics'.
Important: PRD and roadmap contain strategic decisions that you make, not Claude. Use Claude for structure and wording — not for making product decisions.
ruc-4.tip: The best PRD workflow: first describe the problem to Claude in your own words in 5 sentences. Ask it to ask clarifying questions. Answer them. Only then ask for the document draft.
ruc-4.validate: You have used Claude to synthesise real data (interviews or notes) and received structured output that became the basis for a product decision or document.

ruc-5.title: Customer Success: scale without losing quality
ruc-5.why: A CS specialist handles many customers simultaneously — response quality inevitably drops under load. Claude helps maintain a high level at greater volume.
instructions: Response templates with personalisation: create a library of templates for the top 10 request types. Each template is a prompt with variables: customer name, product, issue summary, account context. Claude generates a personalised response based on the template in seconds.

Escalation: 'Here is the correspondence thread with the customer: [HISTORY]. The customer is expressing [DISSATISFACTION LEVEL]. Write: (1) a brief summary of the situation for the manager, (2) the proposed solution with justification, (3) a draft response to the customer'.

Health Score Analysis: 'Here is product usage data for the customer over the last 90 days: [DATA]. What patterns indicate churn risk? Which indicate expansion potential? Suggest 3 specific action items for the CS manager'.

QBR preparation: 'Here is the account data for the quarter: [DATA]. Help prepare a QBR: (1) key achievements that matter specifically to this customer, (2) ROI visualisation, (3) recommendations for the next quarter, (4) open questions for discussion'.

Boundary of application: Claude does not see the relationship history with the customer that you have built. Always provide factual details (figures, agreements, names) explicitly — never assume Claude 'knows' the customer.
ruc-5.tip: The fastest win for CS: create a template for the most frequent request type. The first hour of setup pays off in the first week.
ruc-5.validate: You have a ready response template for at least one request type that you have tested on real cases and it requires minimal editing before sending.

ruc-6.title: Build your role playbook
ruc-6.why: Scattered prompts living in notes do not produce a systemic effect. A playbook turns them into a standard — your personal one or your team's.
instructions: Role playbook structure: (1) Top 5 role tasks with prompts, (2) Recommended Project structure (instructions + knowledge base), (3) Common mistakes to avoid, (4) How to assess output quality, (5) What to never delegate to Claude.
Choose your top 5 scenarios: list five tasks you do every week. For each write a prompt, add an example input and expected output. This is the core of the playbook.
Document anti-patterns: record 2–3 cases where Claude gave a bad result and why. This is the most valuable part of the playbook for colleagues — they learn from your mistakes, not their own.
Format for sharing: a Claude Project with instructions is ideal for storing a playbook. Share access with the team — or export as a Notion/Confluence page with prompts ready to copy.
Living document: add a 'last updated' date and a 15-minute retrospective once a month. Claude and its capabilities change — the playbook must change with them.
ruc-6.tip: The best playbook is minimal but used. Five well-described scenarios beat twenty formal ones. Start small and add as you use it in real work.
ruc-6.validate: You have a role playbook with at least three documented scenarios that you are ready to send to a colleague today. Check: could they use it without your explanations?

role-use-cases.trigger: Basics are solid — time to assemble a working stack for a specific role (Marketing / Sales / HR / Product / CS).
inputs: Your function and top 5 weekly tasks
outputs: Role playbook: 5 tasks × ready prompt + Project
Integration map (MCP / KB / templates)
Onboarding plan for peers in the same role

mcp-advanced.title: Advanced MCP: build your own server
mcp-advanced.subtitle: From ready integrations to a production-grade server you own
mcp-advanced.whatItIs:
Off-the-shelf [[node:mcp|MCP]] servers cover 80% of cases. But sooner or later you hit it: an internal service, a legacy DB with a custom schema, a gated API, non-standard auth — no server exists. So you write your own.

Your own MCP is not "hello world in 50 lines". It is a backend component living next to production: transport, schemas, errors, retries, observability, security. This workflow is how to build it so it is not embarrassing in a registry and does not page you at 3 AM.
mcp-advanced.approach: First take the gateway decision (existing vs your own), then a minimal server on the SDK, then layer in resources/prompts, HTTP transport, Inspector, security, publish. Do not write everything at once — grow in layers, each step validated in Inspector.
outcomes: You understand when MCP is the right answer and when it is not
You built a working server on the official TypeScript or Python SDK
You distinguish tools / resources / prompts and know where each belongs
You run stdio and HTTP/SSE transports and understand the trade-off
You debug through MCP Inspector, not through console.log
You closed the security checklist: scopes, sandboxing, secrets, rate limits
You published the server to a registry or internal NPM/PyPI

applyIn.title: Internal data sources
applyIn.description: Your DB, internal REST, gRPC service — expose to Claude without a public API.

applyIn.title: Domain tooling
applyIn.description: Team-custom tools: code search, build system, deploy pipeline.

applyIn.title: Compliance scenarios
applyIn.description: Data cannot leave for SaaS — sandbox server locally, audit log every call.

pitfalls: Writing your own server before understanding the spec — you rewrite it later.
Putting everything in tools — resources and prompts exist for a reason.
Choosing HTTP transport when stdio is enough — auth, TLS, deploy for zero gain.
Ignoring Inspector — debugging through a client is 10× slower.
Exposing tools with broad scopes ("delete_all") without a confirm flow.

exercises.question: Take an internal team API and wrap it in an MCP server with 2 tools and 1 resource. Drive it through Inspector until green.
exercises.hint: Start with read-only tools. Add write operations as a separate step — easier to review.

exercises.question: Compare stdio and HTTP transport for your server. Measure latency, deploy convenience, auth complexity. Make a decision and record the reasoning.
exercises.hint: stdio = local, zero-config, no auth. HTTP = remote, multi-tenant, needs auth. Not "better", different niches.

s1.title: Gateway decision: build your own or take an existing one
s1.why: Your own server is maintenance forever. Verify nothing existing fits before you commit.
instructions: Open the Anthropic MCP registry and the community list (awesome-mcp-servers).
Search by service name plus 2-3 synonyms. Servers are often named non-obviously.
If found — check last commit, open issues, scope. Forking an existing one beats writing from scratch.
If an existing server is missing one operation — open a PR, do not fork. Saves you a year of maintenance.
If nothing fits — write down the 3-5 operations you actually need (not "all of the API").

Example. Internal trace-storage: nothing exists (checked awesome-mcp-servers, npm, PyPI); needed search_traces, get_trace, get_service_map; NOT needed delete and admin operations. Decision: build my own, scope read-only, 3 tools.
Not sure what the spec covers? Open modelcontextprotocol.io/specification — Server features section. Map your list: what is a tool, what is a resource, what is a prompt.
s1.validate: There is a written list of 3-5 operations and a rationale for why existing servers do not fit.
s1.tip: If an existing server is missing one operation — open a PR, do not fork. Saves you a year of maintenance.

s2.title: Minimal server on the SDK + distributing tools/resources/prompts
s2.why: The official SDK handles transport, JSON-RPC, lifecycle — a hand-rolled protocol on sockets is a month of work and bugs. And the spec gives three primitives for a reason: stuff everything into tools and the client cannot cache or surface things to the user properly.
instructions: Pick a language: TypeScript (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) or Python (`mcp`). Use the one you already have infra for.
Scaffold: `npm init mcp-server` or clone the official quickstart template.
Declare ONE tool with a minimal schema and a stub response. No business logic yet.
Run via stdio (`node dist/index.js`), confirm the process stays up.

Distribute the primitives. Tools = actions with side-effects or computation (search, create, calculate) — the model calls them as needed. Resources = data readable by URI (files, DB records, documents) — the client can pre-fetch and show to the user. Prompts = workflow templates the user explicitly picks ("do a code review"), parameterized.

Walk through your list: each operation lands in one of the three. In doubt — tool (most compatible, supported by all clients). Resource vs tool: "would the client want to show this object BEFORE the model mentions it?" If yes — resource.

Distribution example for trace-storage: search_traces → tool (has parameters, computation); get_trace(id) → resource (`trace://abc123`) — client caches; review_incident → prompt (template: "analyze trace X vs baseline Y").

If `TypeError: Cannot find module @modelcontextprotocol/sdk` — run `npm i @modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, make sure package.json has `"type": "module"`. If the process exits immediately — you forgot `await server.connect(transport)`: without `await` the process closes before connection.
s2.validate: Server starts, does not crash, responds to `tools/list`; each operation is mapped to one of three primitives with a written rationale.
s2.tip: In doubt about a primitive — tool. Most compatible primitive, supported by all clients.

s3.title: Debug through MCP Inspector
s3.why: Inspector is the official MCP devtools. Shows JSON-RPC traffic, schema validation, responses. Without it debugging is `console.log` in the dark.
instructions: Launch Inspector: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node dist/index.js`.
A web UI opens on localhost. You see capabilities, tools, resources.
Call each tool with test parameters from the UI. Look at request/response JSON.
Test edge cases: empty params, wrong type, missing required.
Capture found bugs — fix before the next step.
Inspector can also inspect HTTP servers: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --transport http http://localhost:3000`. Useful before deploy.

If Inspector does not connect — check the server writes to stderr, not stdout (stdout is reserved for JSON-RPC). If a tool responds but Inspector shows a schema error — your response does not match the declared outputSchema: either align the response or drop outputSchema (it is optional).
s3.validate: All declared tools/resources are callable through Inspector with correct responses.
s3.tip: Inspector can also inspect HTTP servers: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --transport http http://localhost:3000`. Useful before deploy.

s4.title: HTTP/SSE transport — when and how
s4.why: stdio is great for local dev and Claude Desktop. For a shared team server or remote deploy you need HTTP with SSE for streaming.
instructions: Decide: HTTP is justified if the server is shared (multiple clients) or hosted remotely.
Use `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` from the SDK — it handles SSE.
Add auth middleware: bearer token in header, OAuth, mTLS — pick per security model.
A `/health` endpoint separate from the MCP route — needed for load balancers.
Log a request-id with each response for tracing.

If the SSE connection drops after 30 sec — a proxy (nginx/cloudflare) closes idle: set `proxy_read_timeout 3600s` or enable keep-alive ping in the SDK. CORS errors from a browser client — add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for known origins; do NOT set `*` in prod — leak vulnerability.
s4.validate: Server returns 401 without a token, 200 with a valid one; Inspector connects over HTTP and sees all tools.
s4.tip: Do not set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` in prod — it is a leak vulnerability. List only known origins.

s5.title: Security: scopes, sandboxing, secrets
s5.why: An MCP server is RCE surface for an LLM. One careless tool with `exec()` and the model can wipe prod.
instructions: Token scoping: the token in env — verify minimum permissions upstream. Not a root key.
Sandboxing: if a tool runs code/shell — isolate (Docker, firejail, vm2). Never `child_process.exec` on raw params from the model.
Confirm flow for destructive: tools with DELETE/UPDATE — explicit confirmation in response ("call confirm_delete with the same id").
Per-tool rate limits: otherwise the model burns quota in a loop.
Audit log: every tool call into structured logs with timestamp, params, result summary, caller id.
Secrets: only via env, never in code. Use a secret manager (1Password / AWS SM / Vault) to inject.

Bad vs good example:
Bad:
```ts
{ name: "run_query", handler: (args) => db.query(args.sql) } // SQL injection via the model
```

Good:
```ts
{
  name: "search_users",
  inputSchema: { properties: { email: { type: "string", format: "email" } } },
  handler: (args) => db.query("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = $1", [args.email])
}
```
If the model spams a tool in a loop — either a bug in logic (tool returns "retry") or rate limit needed: add a circuit breaker, after N consecutive identical calls return error.
s5.validate: The security checklist (6 items above) is filled in, each done/skip with rationale.
s5.tip: Threat model: "what happens if the model tries to harm you?" Not paranoia — prompt injection through resources is real.

s6.title: Publish to registry
s6.why: Without publishing the server only lives on your machine. Registry = distribution + discovery + versioning.
instructions: Prepare README: what it does, which tools, env vars, install command, minimal example config for Claude Desktop.
Version with semver. 0.x while API breaks, 1.0 = public stable.
Publish to npm (TypeScript) or PyPI (Python) with prefix `mcp-server-` or scoped `@org/mcp-*`.
Submit a PR to `modelcontextprotocol/servers` (community) OR your internal registry.
Add CI: every PR runs `inspector` smoke test and schema validation.
Internal server? Host in a private registry (npm Enterprise, internal PyPI). Do not push to public — leaks inner workings.
s6.validate: The server installs via `npx @org/mcp-name`, the config connects to Claude Desktop, tools are visible.
s6.tip: Internal server? Host in a private registry (npm Enterprise, internal PyPI). Do not push to public — leaks inner workings.

mcp-advanced.trigger: No existing MCP server covers your case: internal service, custom auth, specific data schema.
inputs: Access to the upstream API/service you are wrapping
Understanding of the MCP spec (see modelcontextprotocol.io)
outputs: Production-ready MCP server with tools/resources/prompts
Working stdio + HTTP transport
Published package in a registry with README and CI
mcp-advanced.savings: Your own server stops the team copy-pasting from internal tools — ~5-10 hours per week saved.

claude-code-project.title: Production-grade project with Claude Code
claude-code-project.subtitle: CLAUDE.md, hooks, subagents, MCP — a big project that does not turn into chaos
claude-code-project.whatItIs:
[[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] out of the box is already powerful. But in a big project without setup it quickly becomes the "smart but unpredictable teammate": breaks style, goes the wrong direction, burns tokens on the same thing.

A production-grade setup turns Claude Code into a reliable contributor: knows your architecture, does not touch what is off-limits, specializes per task, sees your internal tools, gets verified on every commit.
claude-code-project.approach: In layers. First the CLAUDE.md hierarchy (context and rules), then slash commands (repeatable operations), then guard-rails (hooks + permission policy), subagents (specialization), MCP (integrations), and finally headless mode for CI. Each layer is verified separately.
outcomes: You build a CLAUDE.md hierarchy (root → area → package) without duplication
You author custom slash commands for repeatable team workflows
You configure [[node:cc-hooks|hooks]] (pre/post-tool-use) for lint, audit, secret scan
You deploy [[node:cc-subagents|subagents]] for specialization (reviewer, test-writer, debugger)
You wire MCP to the team's internal services
You set up a permission policy (allow/deny) with a safe default
You run Claude Code in headless mode in CI

applyIn.title: Monorepo with 10+ packages
applyIn.description: CLAUDE.md hierarchy + per-package overrides — Claude respects local rules.

applyIn.title: Code review automation
applyIn.description: Subagent + headless mode in CI — review comments on PRs without human-in-the-loop for routine.

applyIn.title: On-call incident helper
applyIn.description: MCP to logs/metrics + slash command `/incident` → fast triage.

pitfalls: One giant CLAUDE.md of 2000 lines — the model partially ignores it.
Hooks that do not return exit code 0 correctly — they block all tool calls.
Subagents for every micro-task — overhead exceeds the benefit.
Permission policy `allow all` in headless CI — sooner or later it bites.
Forgetting `.claude/settings.local.json` in .gitignore — you commit secrets.

exercises.question: Set up a 3-level CLAUDE.md hierarchy (root, area, package). Verify Claude sees the context at each level — ask a question inside the package and ask it to cite rules.
exercises.hint: Do not duplicate — children only delta from the parent.

exercises.question: Configure a pre-tool-use hook that blocks `git push --force` to main. Break it on purpose — Claude must get an error, explain it, suggest an alternative.
exercises.hint: Hook exit code 2 = block with a message for the model.

s1.title: CLAUDE.md hierarchy
s1.why: CLAUDE.md is persistent context. Without a hierarchy in a monorepo everything is in one file — the model drowns.
instructions: Root `/CLAUDE.md` — global rules: stack, conventions, what is forbidden.
Area-level `/apps/web/CLAUDE.md` — specifics of that area (front, back, infra).
Package-level `/packages/auth/CLAUDE.md` — only delta from parent (package specifics).
Rule: child does not repeat parent, only extends/refines.
Size: root ≤ 200 lines, children ≤ 100. If bigger — move to `/docs` and link.

Example. /CLAUDE.md (root): `# Stack: TypeScript, pnpm, Turborepo` / `# Conventions: ESM only, no default exports, vitest for tests` / `# Forbidden: any in TS, console.log in production, raw SQL in code (ORM only)`. /apps/web/CLAUDE.md: `# Web app specifics` / `# Routing: TanStack Router (file-based)` / `# State: Zustand for global, React Query for server` / `# Tests: vitest + Testing Library, NO enzyme`.
If Claude ignores some rules — file too long or rules conflicting; shorten, move rare ones to /docs.
s1.validate: The hierarchy is visible to Claude (ask an init-like question — you see it reads multiple CLAUDE.md files).
s1.tip: In CLAUDE.md write "rules", not "tutorials". Long explanations → /docs with a link.

s2.title: Custom slash commands
s2.why: If you repeat the same prompt 3+ times a week — it is a slash command. Saves typing and standardizes.
instructions: Commands live in `.claude/commands/<name>.md`.
Each = markdown with instructions + `$ARGUMENTS` placeholders.
Filename = command name (`.claude/commands/review-pr.md` → `/review-pr`).
At the top of the command — frontmatter with `description`, `allowed-tools`.
Commit to the repo — the command becomes shared for the team.

Example. `.claude/commands/release-notes.md` with frontmatter (`description: Generate release notes from commits since last tag`, `allowed-tools: Bash, Read`) and body: get commits since the last tag via `git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --oneline`, group by type (feat/fix/chore/docs), write a human-readable summary, output in CHANGELOG.md format, version: $ARGUMENTS. Call: `/release-notes v2.4.0`.
s2.validate: `/help` shows your command, the call works, arguments are substituted.
s2.tip: Personal commands — in `~/.claude/commands/`. Project — in the repo. Project matters more: shared workflows = consistency.

s3.title: Guard-rails: hooks and permission policy
s3.why: [[node:cc-hooks|Hooks]] are shell scripts that Claude Code runs before/after tool calls: every Bash, Write, Edit goes through your policy. A permission policy (allow/deny) decides ahead of time what is allowed without asking and what is forbidden always — otherwise you get either "approve all blindly" or "constantly interrupts".
instructions: Hooks and permissions config in `.claude/settings.json` (project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (user).
Hooks: `PreToolUse` can block a tool (exit code 2 = block + message for the model); `PostToolUse` for audit, notifications, does not block.
Matcher — regex on tool name: `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit|MultiEdit`. Hook reads JSON from stdin (tool params), writes JSON to stdout (response/error).

Example settings.json hooks: `PreToolUse` matcher `Bash` → command `.claude/hooks/guard-bash.sh`; `PostToolUse` matcher `Edit|Write` → command `.claude/hooks/secret-scan.sh`. The guard-bash.sh script reads stdin, extracts `.tool_input.command` via jq, and on match against `rm -rf|git push.*--force.*main|DROP TABLE` prints `{"decision": "block", "reason": "Destructive command blocked by policy"}` and exits 2, otherwise exits 0.
Permission policy: `permissions` section in settings.json. `allow` — list of patterns (tool + matcher) allowed without asking. `deny` — list FORBIDDEN always (overrides allow).
Principle: deny — destructive (rm, force push, drop), allow — frequent safe (read, lint, test). Everything else will be asked — those questions signal "add to allow or deny".

Example permissions: allow = [`Bash(npm test:*)`, `Bash(pnpm lint:*)`, `Bash(git status)`, `Bash(git diff:*)`, `Read(**)`, `Edit(src/**)`]; deny = [`Bash(rm -rf:*)`, `Bash(git push --force*)`, `Bash(curl:*sh)`, `Write(.env*)`].

If a hook is silently ignored — check chmod +x on the script and that the path in settings.json is project-root-relative or absolute. If a hook blocks everything — exit code 0 = pass, 2 = block, others = warning; check the exit code at the end of the script.
If Claude still asks on allowed — the matcher did not match: `Bash(npm test)` ≠ `Bash(npm test -- --watch)`; use `:*` for wildcards (`Bash(npm test:*)`).
s3.validate: Ask Claude to run a forbidden command (`git push --force`) — it gets a deny/error with your explanation. An allow command (e.g. `npm test`) — runs without asking.
s3.tip: Project settings (committed) = team policy. Personal (`settings.local.json`, in .gitignore) = your individual permissions.

s4.title: Subagents: specialization
s4.why: [[node:cc-subagents|Subagents]] = separate context with a narrow role (reviewer, test-writer, debugger). They keep the main chat clean and solve the task better due to a focused prompt.
instructions: A subagent lives in `.claude/agents/<name>.md` (project) or `~/.claude/agents/` (user).
Frontmatter: `name`, `description` (when to invoke), `tools` (whitelist), optional `model`.
Body — the subagent's system prompt: role, style, output format.
Claude Code decides when to call a subagent (from the description) — or you call `@<name>` explicitly.
One subagent = one narrow task. Not a "universal assistant".

Example. `.claude/agents/test-writer.md` with frontmatter (`name: test-writer`, `description: Write vitest unit tests for new/modified TypeScript functions`, `tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash`, `model: sonnet`) and body: "You write vitest unit tests. Rules: one *.test.ts file per module; AAA structure (Arrange/Act/Assert); mock via `vi.mock`, not hand-rolled factories; cover happy path, edge cases, error path; do not write integration tests — that is another agent."
If a subagent is not auto-invoked — description too generic or conflicts with another agent; make it concrete: "vitest unit tests for TypeScript modules".
s4.validate: Say "write tests for src/auth/token.ts" — the main chat delegates to test-writer, you see it in the log.
s4.tip: A subagent should not "think for you" — it should execute clearly bounded work. If the description is vague, the main chat will not invoke it.

s5.title: MCP to internal services
s5.why: Without [[node:mcp|MCP]] Claude Code only knows files and shell. With MCP — it sees your tracker, docs, DB, metrics.
instructions: Config — `.mcp.json` at the project root (project-scoped, goes to git) OR `~/.claude/mcp.json` (user).
For each MCP server: `command`, `args`, `env`. Secrets via `${ENV_VAR}`, do not hardcode.
Check token scopes — prefer read-only over admin.
After adding — `/mcp` in Claude Code → you see connection status and tool list.
If you have your own server (see "Advanced MCP") — publish internally and connect here.

Example. `.mcp.json` with `mcpServers`: `linear` (command `npx`, args `["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-linear"]`, env `{ "LINEAR_API_KEY": "${LINEAR_API_KEY}" }`) and `internal-traces` (command `npx`, args `["-y", "@acme/mcp-trace-storage"]`, env `{ "TRACE_API_KEY": "${TRACE_API_KEY}" }`). Secrets come from `.envrc` (direnv): `export LINEAR_API_KEY=$(op read "op://Eng/linear/api-key")` and `export TRACE_API_KEY=$(op read "op://Eng/traces/api-key")`.
If a server is connected but tools are empty — the server started but declared no capabilities; check server logs via `claude --mcp-debug` or call the server manually via Inspector.
s5.validate: `/mcp` shows all servers connected, tools visible.
s5.tip: Secrets — only via `${ENV_VAR}` from a secrets manager, never hardcode in `.mcp.json`. Keep token scopes read-only.

s6.title: Headless mode in CI
s6.why: Claude Code is not only interactive. `claude -p` (headless) is a full CLI for CI: code review on PRs, auto-fix lint, generate changelog.
instructions: Headless syntax: `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format json`.
Auth in CI: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env (via GitHub Secrets).
Permissions in CI: explicit `--permission-mode acceptEdits` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions` (only in sandbox CI runner!).
Output: stream JSON — parse in your action.
Time budget: max 5-10 min per run, otherwise CI becomes a bottleneck.

Example. `.github/workflows/claude-review.yml`: trigger `on: pull_request`, job `review` on `ubuntu-latest` with permissions `contents: read` and `pull-requests: write`. Steps: `actions/checkout@v4` with `fetch-depth: 0`, then `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` with `api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}`, `mode: review`, prompt "Review the diff against main. Focus: bugs/edge cases, missing error handling, test coverage gaps. Skip: style/formatting (handled by linters). Post inline comments." and `allowed-tools: "Read,Bash(git diff:*),Bash(pnpm test:*)"`.

If the action exceeds the timeout — reduce scope in prompt ("only diff, not the whole file"), shrink allowed-tools, set max-turns. Permission denied on Bash in CI — the CI sandbox is isolated, there `--permission-mode acceptEdits` is safe, but do NOT use it on a self-hosted runner in prod.
s6.validate: PR opens → action runs → you see inline comments from Claude within 5 minutes.
s6.tip: Cost control: in CI use model `sonnet` (not opus) for routine tasks + `--max-tokens` cap. Otherwise budget blows up.

claude-code-project.trigger: The team uses Claude Code but without rules each developer configures it differently — no consistency, no guard-rails in CI.
inputs: CI runner (GitHub Actions / GitLab CI / etc.)
outputs: CLAUDE.md hierarchy, shared slash commands, hooks, subagents
MCP integrations with team services
Headless Claude Code in CI with code review automation
claude-code-project.savings: A team of 8 devs saves ~15 hours per week on routine code review and chore tasks.

building-evaluations.title: Building evaluations: measuring AI quality
building-evaluations.subtitle: From "seems to work" to reproducible metrics and regression detection
building-evaluations.whatItIs:
Production AI without evals is "deploy and pray". You changed a prompt, swapped a model, updated RAG — how do you know it got better? That you did not break old cases?

[[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|Evals]] are your test suite for an LLM system: a fixed set of tasks, a way to score answers, a metric, CI. Not harder than unit tests, but fundamentally changes how you work: numbers instead of guesses, run-vs-run diffs instead of "seems ok".
building-evaluations.approach: First the golden dataset (small but quality), then the scorer (rule or LLM judge), then the agg metric, then regression detection, finally CI. Do not start with "100 cases and a custom framework" — start with 20 cases and a shell script. Quality grows over time.
outcomes: A golden dataset of 20-50 examples with reference answers
You know when rule-based scorer applies and when LLM-as-judge does
You compute an agg metric (accuracy, F1, custom rubric)
You do run-vs-run diff and see regressions
You integrate evals into CI: a PR with promptlib changes → auto-eval
You balance cost vs quality of the eval run

applyIn.title: Promptlib regression
applyIn.description: Every prompt change is evaluated — regressions caught before merge.

applyIn.title: Model migration
applyIn.description: Sonnet 4 → 4.5: one eval run = decision "migrate or wait".

applyIn.title: RAG tuning
applyIn.description: You change chunk size / embedding / retriever — eval on retrieval+answer shows what improved.

pitfalls: A dataset of 5 examples — statistics meaningless, need ≥ 20.
LLM-as-judge for strictly-formatted tasks (instead of regex) — expensive and noisy.
Eval without a baseline — unclear whether better or worse.
Eval run on every commit — budget blows. Do it on PR or nightly.
Tracking only the average score — you miss regressions on specific cases.

exercises.question: Take one production prompt. Build 20 examples (input + expected output / criterion). Run with the current prompt — what is the baseline accuracy?
exercises.hint: If accuracy is 95%+ — the dataset is too easy. Add edge cases.

exercises.question: Swap the model (e.g. sonnet → haiku) and run the same dataset. Compare results. Is the cost saving worth the quality loss?
exercises.hint: Look not only at avg, but where exactly haiku fails — perhaps on a specific type of case.

be-1.title: Golden dataset: quality > quantity
be-1.why: An eval is only as good as the dataset is representative. 20 right cases beat 200 random ones.
instructions: Write down 5-7 task types your system solves in prod (from logs, not imagination).
For each type — 3-5 examples: 1 happy path, 2 typical, 1-2 edge cases.
For each: input (exactly as in prod) + either exact expected output or a "correctness criterion".
Store as JSONL or CSV — not Excel. Must diff in git.
Version (`evals/v1/dataset.jsonl`) — do not discard the old dataset.
be-1.validate: Dataset covers all main intent classes from prod, has edge cases, lives in git.
be-1.tip: Source of cases — production logs (if compliance allows) + support tickets + user claims. Do NOT invent — reality always differs.

troubleshoot.No idea what edge cases to add: Look at production errors over a month. What did the system answer wrong? Those are your edge cases.

be-2.title: Scorer: rule-based vs LLM-as-judge
be-2.why: The scorer is how you decide "answer is right". Choosing between rule (regex/equality) and LLM judge (another LLM judges) is the critical cost/precision trade-off.
instructions: Rule-based if exact match exists: classification labels, JSON shape, numeric values, format validation.
LLM-as-judge if subjective: explanation quality, tone, factual correctness in free-form text.
Hybrid: rule for structure (JSON valid, contains field X) + LLM for substance.
For LLM judge: use a different model (or at least a different prompt), fixed 1-5 rubric, structured output.
Calibrate judge: take 10 cases with human ratings, verify correlation ≥ 0.7.
be-2.validate: Every case in the dataset has a scorer function (or classification of scorer type).
be-2.tip: For CI prefer rule-based — cheaper and deterministic. LLM judge for weekly deep evals.

troubleshoot.LLM judge gives different scores on the: Set `temperature=0`, fix seed if supported, use structured output. If still noisy — simplify the rubric (5 levels → 3).

be-3.title: Run loop and agg metric
be-3.why: A run = (model, prompt) applied to (dataset) → aggregated metrics. Without aggregation you only see scattered scores.
instructions: Loop: for each record in dataset — call the system, scorer, save {id, input, output, score, metadata}.
Save full run to a file with timestamp and git SHA: `evals/runs/2026-05-27-abc1234.jsonl`.
Agg metrics: avg score, % above threshold, breakdown by task type, by edge_case=true/false.
Parallelism: use async (`asyncio.gather` / `Promise.all`) — but with rate limiting.
Cost tracking: count input+output tokens, $ estimate per run.
be-3.example:
run_eval.py:
```python
import asyncio, json, time, subprocess
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

async def run_case(client, case, system_prompt):
    resp = await client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
        max_tokens=500,
        system=system_prompt,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case["input"]}]
    )
    return {
        "id": case["id"],
        "output": resp.content[0].text,
        "input_tokens": resp.usage.input_tokens,
        "output_tokens": resp.usage.output_tokens
    }

async def main():
    sha = subprocess.check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"]).decode().strip()
    dataset = [json.loads(l) for l in open("evals/dataset.jsonl")]
    client = AsyncAnthropic()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*[run_case(client, c, SYSTEM) for c in dataset])
    for r, c in zip(results, dataset):
        r["score"] = score(r["output"], c["expected"])
    out = f"evals/runs/{int(time.time())}-{sha}.jsonl"
    with open(out, "w") as f:
        for r in results: f.write(json.dumps(r) + "\n")
    avg = sum(r["score"] for r in results) / len(results)
    cost = sum(r["input_tokens"] * 3 + r["output_tokens"] * 15 for r in results) / 1_000_000
    print(f"avg={avg:.3f}  cost=${cost:.4f}  saved={out}")

asyncio.run(main())
```
be-3.validate: A run produces a file with per-case scores, aggregated avg, and cost.

troubleshoot.Rate limit errors: Add a semaphore: `sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)` and wrap calls. Or use the Batch API for non-realtime evals — 50% discount.

be-4.title: Regression detection: run-vs-run diff
be-4.why: Avg score went from 0.82 to 0.84 — success? Maybe you fixed 5 cases and broke 3. Diff shows the truth.
instructions: Diff = join by `id` of two runs → score delta per case.
Categorize: improved, regressed (score dropped), stable, new (not in baseline).
Threshold: regression significant if score drops by ≥ 0.2 on a specific case or ≥ 0.05 on average per category.
If ≥ 1 significant regression — fail the PR, require review.
Output — markdown table in PR comment with the specific regressed cases (input, old output, new output).
be-4.validate: Diff between two runs produces a readable report; a PR with regressions fails.
be-4.tip: Keep "accepted regressions" (e.g. an edge case you are willing to accept) in a separate allowlist. Diff ignores them.

be-5.title: CI integration
be-5.why: An eval that does not run automatically dies over time. CI is the only way to keep it alive.
instructions: Trigger: on PR that changes files in `prompts/`, `evals/`, `src/llm/`.
Steps: run eval → diff vs baseline (last main run) → comment on PR.
Store baseline as an artifact or commit it under `evals/runs/main/`.
API key via secrets, NOT in code/config.
Timeout: 10-15 min max. If dataset is large — Batch API or sample (random 30 cases).
be-5.example:
.github/workflows/eval.yml:
```yaml
name: Eval
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["prompts/**", "src/llm/**", "evals/dataset.jsonl"]

jobs:
  eval:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.11" }
      - run: pip install anthropic
      - name: Run eval
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
        run: python evals/run_eval.py | tee eval-output.txt
      - name: Diff vs baseline
        run: python evals/diff_runs.py evals/runs/main/latest.jsonl evals/runs/$(ls -t evals/runs | head -1)
      - uses: marocchino/sticky-pull-request-comment@v2
        if: always()
        with:
          path: eval-output.txt
```
be-5.validate: PR with a prompt change → action runs, posts a comment with avg, cost, and diff.

troubleshoot.CI eval fails intermittently: Network errors to the API. Add retry with exponential backoff (3 tries), tenacity style.

be-6.title: Cost-quality trade-off and where the lines are
be-6.why: A perfect eval is infinitely expensive. A real one balances cost vs signal. Without an explicit trade-off the budget blows up and evals get turned off.
instructions: Budget per run = $0.10-$1 for CI (on PR), $5-$20 for weekly deep eval.
Sampling: 30-50 cases for PR (fast feedback), full dataset for nightly/weekly.
Tiered evals: smoke (5 cases, $0.01, on every commit) → full (50 cases, on PR) → deep (200 + LLM judge, weekly).
Caching: same input + same prompt — cache the answer. Only changes when prompt/model changes.
Batch API for non-realtime — half price, up to 24h delay.
be-6.example:
Triggers:
- commit → smoke (5 cases, $0.01, 30 sec) — on pre-commit hook
- PR → fast (30 cases, rule-based, $0.30, 2 min) — github action
- nightly main → full (50 cases, $0.80, 5 min) — cron
- weekly → deep (200 cases + LLM judge, $15, 30 min) — manual / schedule

This split covers 90% of cases at a reasonable cost.
be-6.validate: You have a written budget for evals (per PR / per week) and a tiering that fits in it.
be-6.tip: When the product is stable — deep eval may be monthly, not weekly. Measure eval ROI (bugs caught) — that is the argument for management that the budget is justified.

building-evaluations.trigger: Your production AI system changes and it is unclear if each change makes it better or worse — you need a measurable feedback loop.
inputs: 20-50 real cases with reference answers / criteria
outputs: Golden dataset in git, versioned
Run script + scorer + agg metrics
CI workflow with regression detection and PR comments

tools.name: Anthropic SDK
tools.role: invoke models in the eval loop

building-evaluations.savings: Eval catches ~80% of regressions before prod. One prevented incident pays for a quarter of evals.

remote-computer-for-claude.title: Build a remote computer for Claude
remote-computer-for-claude.subtitle: An isolated environment where the agent controls a PC — not yours
remote-computer-for-claude.whatItIs: A step-by-step build of a safe environment where [[node:cap-computer|Claude controls a computer]] inside an isolated “box” instead of on your real machine. We use Anthropic's reference Computer Use container (Docker + a desktop in the browser). After this tutorial you'll be able to set up such a system at home and safely give the agent tasks.
remote-computer-for-claude.approach: The core principle: the agent NEVER works where your personal files, passwords and work network are. Isolation first — tasks second. Don't mount home folders, don't type real passwords, keep a kill-switch and a spending cap at hand.
outcomes: An isolated environment with computer use is up
Claude acts inside the box, visible in the browser
Privileges, network, secrets, rollback and a kill-switch are set
You understand how to move this to a cloud VM

applyIn.title: GUI automation without an API
applyIn.description: The agent clicks in legacy software or web panels that have no API — but in a safe sandbox.

applyIn.title: Safe experiments
applyIn.description: You try autonomous scenarios without risking your personal machine and data.

pitfalls: Running computer use directly on your personal PC that has access to email and banking.
Mounting home folders or real secrets into the container — isolation is lost.
Giving the agent real passwords instead of one-time accounts.
Leaving the container's port open to the public internet without a password.

exercises.question: Bring up the container and give the agent a safe task: “open a text editor and type Hello”. Make sure it acts only inside the environment.
exercises.hint: Watch the agent's desktop in the browser at http://localhost:8080. If it succeeded and nothing outside the container was touched — step done.

exercises.question: Take a snapshot of the clean state and roll back to it after the task.
exercises.hint: For Docker, recreating the container from the image already gives a clean state; for a VM, use the provider's snapshot.

remote-computer-for-claude.trigger: You want to give Claude computer use but fear for your machine and data.
inputs: A computer with Docker, or a cloud VM
An Anthropic API key (separate, with a spending cap)
A browser to view the agent's desktop
outputs: An isolated Claude Computer Use environment
A safety checklist before production use
remote-computer-for-claude.savings: Days of trial-and-error and risk to your personal PC → a managed sandbox in ~1.5 hours

s1.title: Why isolation: threat model and choosing a host
s1.why: Without a clear goal it's easy to build insecurely. The goal is a “box” where the agent is isolated from your personal data, passwords and work network.
instructions: Read the node [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|Isolated environment for the agent]] — it is the map of the topic.
Remember the rule: the agent must have no access to personal data, passwords or the work network.
Threat model: the agent sees the screen, clicks and types — so it can open your email, bank, or exfiltrate files if they are reachable. Isolation removes that reachability.
Choose a host. Your PC + Docker: free and fast, but works only while the PC is on.
Cloud VM (VPS): runs around the clock, but is paid and needs remote access. See [[node:sas-vm-vps|VM or dedicated PC]].
For learning, start with your PC — the most reproducible path; moving to a VM is step s5.
s1.validate: You can explain why the agent needs a separate environment, and you've chosen a host understanding its trade-offs.
s1.tip: Isolation first — tasks second. Not the other way around.

s2.title: Docker and the reference Computer Use container
s2.why: Docker is the “box” that isolates the agent from your system. Anthropic's reference container is the official sandbox: the desktop and agent are already inside, nothing is installed on your system.
instructions: Download Docker Desktop (Windows/Mac) or Docker Engine (Linux) from docker.com, install and start it.
Check in the terminal: `docker --version`.
Run a test container: `docker run hello-world` — it should print a greeting.
Open the anthropic-quickstarts repo → the computer-use-demo folder — it has the current command, image name and ports (they can change).

Run the container, passing the key via the environment. Roughly: `docker run -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -p 8080:8080 -it <computer-use-demo-image>` — take the exact ports from the README.
Wait for the container to come up (the interface address appears in the logs). The key is set up in step s4 — come back here after it if you haven't set the variable yet.
s2.validate: `docker run hello-world` ran without errors, the reference container is running, and there are no errors about the key or ports in the logs.
s2.tip: Take the image name and ports from the computer-use-demo README — they can change between versions.

s3.title: noVNC: the agent's desktop in the browser and a first task
s3.why: Through the browser (noVNC) you see the agent's screen — your “CCTV” and control. See [[node:sas-remote-access|remote access]]. Control means the ability to stop at any moment.
instructions: Open the interface address from the README or launch logs in the browser (usually one combined URL, e.g. http://localhost:8080).
On the left — the chat with the agent; on the right — the virtual desktop. If it won't open — check the needed port is published (`-p ...`) and not in use.
Give the first safe task: “Open a text editor and type Hello”. Don't give tasks with internet or data access yet.
Watch the cursor move and type by itself on the virtual desktop, and how the agent takes screenshots and clicks step by step.
Find how to stop the agent in the interface (stop/interrupt). Remember: always watch the first runs of a new task.
s3.validate: You see the agent's desktop, it did a harmless task inside the environment (nothing changed on your real PC), and you can stop it mid-task.
s3.tip: Always watch the first runs of a new task live — keep stop within reach.

s4.title: Security: least privilege, network and secrets
s4.why: Even in a container you must not give the agent more than needed: no access to your files, your local network, or secrets in code. See [[node:sas-least-privilege|least privilege]], [[node:sas-network-isolation|network isolation]], [[node:sas-secrets|one-time accounts and secrets]].
instructions: Separate key with a cap: in console.anthropic.com create a NEW API key just for this environment; in Billing/Limits set a monthly spending cap. Don't reuse a key from other projects — a separate one is easy to revoke (see [[node:sas-snapshots-killswitch|kill-switch and caps]]).

Store the key in the environment, not in code: `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-...` (Linux/Mac) or `setx ANTHROPIC_API_KEY "sk-..."` + a new terminal window (Windows). Check: `echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Never commit the key to git and never show it to the agent in a task.

Least privilege: do NOT mount your home folders into the container (no `-v /Users/you:...`). If a task needs files — put only those in a separate folder. Inside the environment, work as a regular user, not root, where possible.
Network: to start, don't give the container access to your local network or router. If a task doesn't need the internet — run the container with `--network none`.
When internet is needed — keep a list of allowed sites (an allowlist) via a proxy/firewall as the goal.
s4.validate: The key is separate, capped, stored in env and not in git; the launch command has no personal-folder mounts; the environment's network access is the minimum needed.
s4.tip: Real passwords — never. Only one-time accounts inside the sandbox.

s5.title: Cloud VM/VPS and remote access (optional)
s5.why: So the environment runs 24/7, independent of your PC.
instructions: Take a cheap cloud VM — a separate one, not a work server. See [[node:sas-vm-vps|VM or dedicated PC]].
Install Docker on the VM and run the same Computer Use container (everything from steps s2–s4 carries over unchanged).
Desktop access — via the browser at the VM's address, protected with a password/key and an IP restriction.
Don't leave the port open to the public internet without a password — it's one of the main risks.
s5.validate: The same container runs on the VM, and access to it is locked with a password/key and restricted by IP.
s5.tip: The VM should be an isolated, disposable one, not your work server.

s6.title: Snapshots, kill-switch and the final checklist
s6.why: Reversibility and control: whatever happens, you put it back and stop it instantly. One pass through the checklist catches most dangerous mistakes. See [[node:sas-snapshots-killswitch|snapshots, rollback and kill-switch]].
instructions: Snapshot and rollback. Docker: a clean state = recreate the container from the image (`docker rm` + `docker run` again). VM: take a snapshot before experiments via the provider. Rule: a new risky task → first fix a clean state.
Kill-switch: `docker stop <container>` instantly halts the agent. Check the spending cap on the key (step s4) is active. Decide in advance: on odd behavior — stop first, investigate later.

Final checklist: home folders are NOT mounted; real passwords are NOT passed; the key is separate, capped, in env, not in code; the network is minimal; the kill-switch and rollback are tested; remote access (if any) is protected with a password/key and an IP restriction.
What's next: go through the [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|Isolated environment for the agent]] path in full, start with simple tasks, and expand access gradually and deliberately.
Practice idea: give the agent a routine GUI task you do by hand — but in the sandbox.
s6.validate: Every checklist item is ticked, you can roll back the environment and stop the agent — the environment is ready to use.
s6.tip: Stop first, investigate second — it's cheaper than the other way around.

claude-workspace.title: Claude's Workspace: Desktop and web from scratch
claude-workspace.subtitle: Three modes, every menu, and Settings — a walkthrough of each item
claude-workspace.whatItIs: A complete walkthrough of the Claude app (Desktop for macOS/Windows and web at [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]): three tabs — Chat, [[node:pl-cowork|Cowork]], and Code — plus the entire Settings screen. After this tutorial you understand what every menu does and can set up your workspace for projects and code deliberately instead of by guesswork.
claude-workspace.approach: We go top to bottom: install → the three modes → working in each → panels and shortcuts → Computer use → a full walkthrough of Settings (General, Account, Privacy, Billing, Usage, Capabilities, Connectors, Claude Code, Cowork) and the Desktop app section (General, Extensions, Developer) → the link with the CLI and troubleshooting.
outcomes: You understand the difference between the three modes — Chat / Cowork / Code — and when to use each
You know the purpose of every Settings item, not just General
You can pick the right permission mode (Ask / Auto accept / Plan / Auto / Bypass) for the task
You connect Connectors (MCP) and Desktop extensions safely
You set up Computer use with a clear understanding of its access boundaries and risks

applyIn.title: Starting work on code
applyIn.description: The Code tab: a session with Git isolation, project folder selection, permission mode, preview, and diff review.

applyIn.title: Long-running and background tasks
applyIn.description: Cowork and remote sessions: launch tasks that keep running even when the app is closed.

applyIn.title: Team onboarding
applyIn.description: A single walkthrough of Settings so colleagues don't get lost in the menus or run into limits.

pitfalls: Thinking Desktop is "just a chat": in reality it's three distinct modes with different capabilities.
Turning on Bypass permissions outside a sandbox — Claude runs commands without confirmation.
Ignoring Settings → Privacy and Capabilities — that's where both your data privacy and the available tools live.
Confusing local and remote sessions: a remote session has no @-files and no access to your local disk.
Enabling Computer use without understanding the app access tiers and the risk of prompt injection from the screen.

exercises.question: Open Chat, Cowork, and Code in turn. Note how the left menu differs in each mode.
exercises.hint: Chat — list of conversations; Cowork — tasks/schedules; Code — sessions.

exercises.question: Go through every Settings section and answer in one sentence: “why do I need it”.
exercises.hint: If you can’t answer, open it and read the caption.

exercises.question: Start your first local Code session in a test folder using Plan mode and review the plan without edits.
exercises.hint: Plan mode explores and proposes a plan without changing source files.

s1.title: Install and the three modes: Chat, Cowork, Code
s1.why: This is the entry point: install sets the requirements, and the three modes are the app’s main fork. Pick the wrong mode and you won’t find the features you need.
instructions: Install: download the app at claude.com/download (macOS — universal, Windows — x64/ARM64; Linux isn’t supported — use the CLI there), launch it and sign in. For the Code tab on Windows you need Git for Windows — install it and restart. Version — macOS: Claude → About Claude, Windows: Help → About.
The web version ([[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]) runs in the browser with no install, but without local files, a terminal, or the Desktop app section.
Chat — a regular conversation (questions, text, working through files); the left menu is the list of conversations. This is where 80% of everyday work happens.
Cowork — agentic and long-running tasks: New task, Projects, Scheduled, Live artifacts, Dispatch (from your phone), Customize.
Code — development: each conversation is a "session" with its own history, project folder, and code changes; the menu has New session, Routines, Customize.
Rule of thumb: ask / write / work through something → Chat; hand off something long-running or scheduled → Cowork; code in a repository → Code. You can switch modes at the top at any time.

Chat composer: input field + Enter, next to it the model picker (e.g. Opus/Sonnet) and the voice button (microphone); model and effort change right inside a conversation. The "+" button on the left: attach files, connect [[node:skills|Skills]], [[node:mcp|Connectors]], and plugins. Drag files straight into the field — Claude works through images and PDFs ([[node:cap-input-modalities|file and image support]]).
s1.validate: The app opened, you’re signed in, you see the three tabs at the top and can explain what each (Chat, Cowork, Code) is for and where the composer’s “+” is.
s1.tip: Desktop and the CLI can live side by side on one machine and even on the same project — they share the same config (CLAUDE.md, MCP). You can switch modes at the top at any time with no data loss.

s2.title: Code mode: starting a session and permission modes
s2.why: Before your first message in Code you need to set up the environment and pick a permission mode — the main safeguard that decides whether Claude asks before edits and commands.
instructions: Environment — where it runs: Local (your machine), Remote (Anthropic’s cloud, keeps going when the app is closed), SSH (your own server).

Project folder — the folder or repository Claude works with; for Remote you can add several repositories. Model — the picker next to the send button, change it as you go. Enter your task and hit Enter.
Ask permissions (default) — asks before every edit/command and shows a diff; recommended for beginners.
Auto accept edits — accepts file edits and safe commands (mkdir, mv) on its own, but asks about other commands.
Plan mode — explores and proposes a plan without touching the source; great for complex "think first" tasks.
Auto — does everything with background safety checks (research preview, requires a recent Opus/Sonnet).
Bypass permissions — no confirmations at all; sandbox/VM only, enabled in Settings → Claude Code.
s2.validate: Before sending you can see the Environment, folder, and model pickers and can pick the right permission mode for the task, knowing which is dangerous outside a sandbox.
s2.tip: A solid workflow: start in Plan → approve the plan → switch to Auto accept edits to carry it out. For long refactors and test runs choose Remote — the task won’t be interrupted even if you close the app.

s3.title: Working with code: context, preview, diff, and review
s3.why: The sharper the context and the better you steer Claude, the less rework you get; and the visual preview and diff review remove “blind” edits.
instructions: @-mention a file: type @ and the name — the file goes into context (not available in Remote).
Attachments: images, PDFs, screenshots of bugs — via the button or by dragging them in. Claude reads the project files, makes edits, and runs commands according to the permission mode you chose.
Interrupting: the stop button halts immediately; or just type a correction and hit Enter — Claude factors it in after the current step.
Preview — Claude spins up a dev server and opens a built-in browser; auto-verification takes screenshots and clicks elements after edits.

Diff: an indicator like "+12 −1" opens the per-file change view; click a line to leave a comment. Submit comments: macOS — Cmd+Enter, Windows — Ctrl+Enter; Claude makes the edits and shows a new diff.
"Review code" in the diff view — Claude looks for bugs, logic issues, and security problems on its own (not style). After a PR, a CI panel appears: Auto-fix and Auto-merge toggles.
s3.validate: You added a file via @, steered Claude with a correction without stopping its work, opened a diff, left a comment, and requested “Review code”.
s3.tip: A short clarifying correction mid-run is cheaper than fully restarting the task. The preview server config lives in .claude/launch.json — that’s where you put your own launch command and port.

s4.title: The workspace: panels, shortcuts, parallel sessions, Computer use
s4.why: Code is built from panels you arrange to suit yourself; parallel sessions and Computer use add power but require understanding isolation and access boundaries.
instructions: Panels: chat, diff, preview, terminal, file, plan, tasks, subagent — open them from the Views menu and drag them by the title.
Terminal: Ctrl+` — opens in the session folder, the same environment Claude uses (npm test, git status). Files: click a path to open the file, make targeted edits + Save.
Transcript modes (Normal/Verbose/Summary) — Ctrl+O. All shortcuts — Cmd+/ (macOS) or Ctrl+/ (Windows).
Parallel sessions: + New session (Cmd+N), Ctrl+Tab switches between them; for Git repositories each session gets its own isolated copy via a worktree — edits don’t overlap until a commit.
