Side-chat (Cmd+; or /btw) — an aside question with the session’s context, without cluttering the main conversation. The Tasks panel shows background work: subagents and background commands.

Computer use — controlling apps on your screen: enabled in Settings → General (Desktop app section) with the Computer use toggle; on macOS it needs Accessibility and Screen Recording; requires a Pro/Max plan (not Team/Enterprise) and a running Desktop app.

Computer use access tiers are fixed: browsers — view only, terminals/IDEs — clicks only, everything else — full control. More on safe, isolated execution — [[node:sys-agent-sandbox|an isolated environment for the agent]] and [[node:cap-computer|Computer use]].
s4.validate: You opened a second panel from Views, switched the transcript mode, opened a second session, and understand which permissions Computer use needs.
s4.tip: Verbose shows every step Claude takes — handy to understand why it did something a certain way. Auto-archive after a merge/closed PR (Settings → Claude Code) clears out finished sessions for you.

s5.title: Settings, part 1: General, Account, Privacy, Billing, Usage, Capabilities
s5.why: These Settings sections define how Claude behaves everywhere, sign-in security, data privacy, money, and the set of available tools.
instructions: General → Profile: name, "what to call you", occupation, and Instructions for Claude — general guidance for all chats and Cowork ([[node:i-global|global instructions]]).

General → Preferences: Appearance (system/light/dark), Chat font. General → Voice (voice style and speed) and Notifications (response completion, Code notifications, permission requests, Dispatch messages).
Account: "Log out of all devices", Organization ID, the list of active sessions (device, city, dates), account deletion.
Privacy — how your data is used and model training; go through this section deliberately ([[node:pl-privacy|privacy]]).
Billing — plan and payment; Usage — usage by period and by model (the plan is shared across all Claude surfaces).
Capabilities — toggles for Claude’s capabilities (web search, analysis, and so on). The usage ring next to the model picker in Code shows the session context and the plan’s overall usage.
s5.validate: You filled in Instructions for Claude, found the active sessions in Account, and know where to check usage (Usage) and toggle capabilities (Capabilities).
s5.tip: Instructions for Claude is the most underrated item: one setting improves tone and format across all conversations. If you’re hitting limits, check Usage and compare models first before upgrading.

s6.title: Settings, part 2 and the Desktop app section: Cowork, Connectors, Claude Code, Extensions, Developer, CLI
s6.why: Here live the Cowork agentic mode, the app’s “sockets” (Connectors/MCP), code-session behavior, local Desktop extensions, and the link with the CLI — everything beyond the browser.
instructions: Cowork: New task sets up a task, "Work in a project" ties it to a [[node:projects|project]] with its knowledge and instructions; Scheduled — recurring tasks on a schedule; Live artifacts — result artifacts that keep updating; Dispatch (Beta) — sending tasks from your phone (requires Pro/Max, not Team/Enterprise); Customize — connectors, skills, and plugins in one place. A detailed walkthrough is in the tutorial [[tutorial:claude-cowork|Claude Cowork]].

Settings → Connectors — integrations (Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, Linear, Notion …): these are [[node:mcp|MCP servers]] with a graphical setup, also added from the "+" in the composer; for services not on the list, add MCP manually via the config files (custom connectors exist too).

Settings → Claude Code — the behavior of Code sessions: allow Bypass permissions, worktree location, auto-archive after a PR, turning Preview and Persist sessions on/off. Settings → Cowork — agentic-mode and Dispatch settings.
The Desktop app → General section: the Computer use toggle, the status of system permissions, Denied apps (apps Claude won’t touch), and "Unhide apps when Claude finishes".

Desktop app → Extensions — install extensions/connectors in one click, no terminal needed. Desktop app → Developer — connect local MCP servers and developer configuration; MCP from the chat app (claude_desktop_config.json) is picked up in the Code tab too.

CLI ↔ Desktop: it’s one engine with shared config (CLAUDE.md, MCP servers ~/.claude.json and .mcp.json, hooks, skills, settings); move a session from the terminal with the /desktop command ([[node:claude-code|CLI]]). What Desktop lacks: third-party providers (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry), Linux, inline suggestions, agent teams, terminal dialogs (/permissions, /config, /agents).

Troubleshooting: 403 — sign out and back in; blank screen — restart/update; on Windows, Code needs Git; if an MCP server isn’t responding on Windows — check the config, restart the app, and see whether the server process is still alive in Task Manager.
s6.validate: You opened Connectors (understanding they’re MCP), found the Computer use toggle in Desktop app → General, and know the first thing to do on a 403 error.
s6.tip: Disconnect/Manage connectors — in Settings → Connectors or via “Manage connectors” in the composer. On a 403, sign out and back in; blank screen — restart/update; on Windows, Code needs Git.

project-files.title: Uploading files to a Project
project-files.subtitle: How to give Claude documents as context and ask questions about them
project-files.whatItIs: A walkthrough of how to upload files to a [[node:projects|Project]] so Claude answers based on your documents — brand guidelines, specs, code, spreadsheets — instead of relying on general knowledge.
project-files.approach: We move from "what Claude can read" → how and where to upload → what belongs in project knowledge versus a chat → how to phrase a request about the files → common mistakes → keeping everything current.
outcomes: Understand which formats Claude can read and how it uses them in its answers
Know the difference between project knowledge and an attachment in a single chat
Can reference a file in your request and get an answer based strictly on it
Avoid duplicates and outdated files that spoil the answers

applyIn.title: Working from a brand guide
applyIn.description: Upload the guide to a Project, and every piece of text is written in your tone of voice.

applyIn.title: Document analysis
applyIn.description: PDF contracts, reports, specs: ask about the contents without copying the text by hand.

applyIn.title: Context for code
applyIn.description: Upload the key files or the schema, and Claude answers with your project in mind.

pitfalls: Dropping a file into a single chat when it's needed across every conversation in the project — it belongs in the Project's knowledge.
Keeping outdated versions of files: Claude will trust the old document.
Uploading dozens of files "just in case" — the extra context dilutes the answer.
Asking about a file without naming it when there are many — specify exactly which one.

exercises.question: Create a Project, upload a single document into its knowledge (for example, a brand guide), and ask a question that can only be answered from that file.
exercises.hint: If Claude answers in general terms, check that the file is in the Project's knowledge, not just attached to a chat.

exercises.question: Compare: ask the same question with the file uploaded and without it. What changed in the answer?
exercises.hint: That difference is exactly the value of context from the file.

pf-1.title: What Claude can read
pf-1.why: Before you upload anything, understand which files are actually useful and how Claude "sees" them.
instructions: Supported formats include PDF, DOCX, text, code, spreadsheets (CSV/XLSX), and images ([[node:cap-input-modalities|file and image support]]).
Claude reads the contents as part of the context: it quotes, summarizes, and answers based on them.
It can also parse images and scans (Vision), but the quality depends on how legible they are.
Large files take up context — this affects how long the conversation can run; don't upload more than you need.
pf-1.validate: You understand which formats to upload and what Claude does with them.
pf-1.tip: If the document is a table of numbers, first ask Claude to restate its structure so you can confirm it read it correctly.

pf-2.title: How and where to upload
pf-2.why: There are two places for files, and your choice determines which conversations Claude will see them in.
instructions: Project knowledge: open the [[node:projects|Project]] → the knowledge/files section → add the document. It's available across every conversation in that project.
Chat attachment: use the attach button or drag the file straight into the input field — the file only lives in that one conversation.
Rule of thumb: permanent and shared → Project knowledge; one-off → chat attachment.
You can drag files in with the mouse, and several at once too.
pf-2.validate: You've added a file to the Project's knowledge and understand how that differs from a chat attachment.
pf-2.tip: If you need the same file again and again, it definitely belongs in the Project's knowledge rather than in each new chat.

pf-3.title: What goes into knowledge versus into a chat
pf-3.why: Project knowledge is the "permanent memory." The stable things go there; the variable things go into a chat.
instructions: Into Project knowledge: brand guide, tone of voice, specs, templates, reference materials — whatever you need all the time.
Into a chat: a one-off document for a specific task (a single contract, one report to review).
The link to [[node:p-instructions|project instructions]]: files are the "what to know," instructions are the "how to behave."
Don't mix them: a dozen one-off files in the knowledge becomes clutter that gets in the way.
pf-3.validate: For any given file, you can decide whether it's permanent (into knowledge) or one-off (into a chat).
pf-3.tip: Set yourself a rule: Project knowledge = only the things that will outlive the current task.

pf-4.title: How to ask about a file
pf-4.why: The file is uploaded — now you need to reference it correctly so the answer stays strictly within the document.
instructions: Name the source: "using the brand guide, write a post…", "based on section 3 of the contract, answer…".
If there are many files, specify exactly which one to answer from.
Ask for verifiability: "quote the passage your answer is based on."
Example: upload the brand guide and ask, "write a 3-paragraph announcement in our tone of voice."
pf-4.validate: You got an answer that clearly draws on the uploaded file rather than on general knowledge.
pf-4.tip: Asking "quote where you got this" quickly reveals whether Claude actually read the file or just made it up.

pf-5.title: Common mistakes
pf-5.why: Most cases of "Claude gives the wrong answer" about files come down to four typical mistakes.
instructions: Outdated file: an old version is sitting there and Claude trusts it. Keep a single current one.
Duplicates: two versions of the same document confuse the model. Delete the extra one.
Overload: dozens of files blur the focus. Keep only what the task needs.
Wrong container: a file attached to a chat isn't visible in the project's other conversations.
pf-5.validate: You recognize these four mistakes and know how to fix each one.
pf-5.tip: If an answer seems off, first check which file is actually uploaded and whether it's out of date.

pf-6.title: Keeping things current
pf-6.why: Files go stale. Project knowledge is only as useful as it is fresh.
instructions: Periodically review the Project's knowledge: replace what's outdated, remove what's unnecessary.
When a document changes substantially, upload the new version and delete the old one.
Keep a "single source of truth": one current file per topic.
Next, set up your [[node:p-instructions|project instructions]] so Claude knows how to use these files.
pf-6.validate: The Project's knowledge holds only current files, one per topic.
pf-6.tip: Tie this to a regular cleanup: an outdated brand guide is worse than no brand guide at all.

project-instructions.title: Project Instructions: set Claude's role once
project-instructions.subtitle: 6 steps to make Claude an expert in exactly your task
project-instructions.whatItIs:
Project Instructions is a text field in [[node:projects|Project]] settings that Claude reads before every reply inside the project. You write once who Claude should be, in what style and format it should answer, and what constraints to keep. After that, every conversation in the project already runs "in role" — no need to repeat instructions in each chat.

This is not the product's system prompt (set by Anthropic) and not [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] (those are about you personally and apply across all chats). Project Instructions are narrow and local: they describe the working context of one specific project.
project-instructions.approach: Write the instruction like a brief for a new hire: role, style, format, constraints. Specificity beats length. One precise line ("structure: Context → Problem → Recommendation") changes answers more than a paragraph of vague wishes like "be helpful".
outcomes: Understand the difference between Project Instructions, the system prompt, and Custom Instructions
Know where the field is and which four blocks to write into it (role / style / format / constraints)
Can remove vagueness and phrase instructions concretely
Have a ready instruction template reusable in any project
Can verify the instruction actually changes answers and keep it up to date

applyIn.title: Work project with a stable role
applyIn.description: Set the analyst, editor, or developer role once — and every chat in the project answers in it without reminders.

applyIn.title: Team project
applyIn.description: The instruction locks in a shared style and format, so answers stay consistent no matter who on the team is writing.

applyIn.title: Recurring type of task
applyIn.description: Regular reports, reviews, or emails get one answer skeleton, defined once in the instruction.

pitfalls: Vague phrases like "be helpful" or "answer professionally" — that's noise that changes nothing.
Mixing personal preferences (which belong in Custom Instructions) with project context in one field.
Writing a half-page wall of text — Claude loses priorities and key rules get buried.
Setting the instruction once and forgetting it — the project's role drifts while the instruction goes stale.
Duplicating in the instruction what already lives in [[node:p-files|project files]] instead of referencing them.

exercises.question: Take your current project and write in one line: who Claude should be, in what format to answer, and what not to do. Did you fit it into three clear phrases?
exercises.hint: If each item turns into a generic phrase with no specifics — add an example of the format or role from a real task.

exercises.question: Run the same question in the project without an instruction and with one. What exactly changed in the answer?
exercises.hint: Compare structure, tone, and language — that's the visible effect of the instruction.

exercises.question: Find the vaguest phrase in your instruction and rewrite it into a concrete rule with an example.
exercises.hint: "Write concisely" → "Answer in up to 5 points, each ≤ 2 sentences".

s1.title: Why Project Instructions matter
s1.why: Without an instruction a project answers like a generic assistant: every chat starts from scratch and you re-explain the role each time. The instruction turns the project into a specialist in your task.
instructions: Grasp the key point: Project Instructions are read before every reply inside the project — persistent context, not a one-off message.
Difference from the system prompt: the system prompt is set by Anthropic, covers safety and base behavior, and you don't change it.
Difference from [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]]: those describe you personally and apply across all chats; Project Instructions are narrow and act only in this project.
Remember the hierarchy: system prompt → Custom Instructions → Project Instructions. The most specific layer is the project.
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence how Project Instructions differ from Custom Instructions.
s1.tip: If a rule is needed in all projects — that's Custom Instructions. If only in one — Project Instructions.

s2.title: Where the field is and what to write
s2.why: Most people drop random wishes into the instruction. A four-block structure makes it complete and checkable from the start.
instructions: Open the [[node:projects|Project]] → project settings → the Instructions block (next to Project knowledge).
Block 1 — role: who Claude acts as ("you're a financial analyst", "you're a technical editor").
Block 2 — style: tone and language of the answer (formal / conversational, English only).
Block 3 — format: the answer's skeleton (structure, length, required sections).
Block 4 — constraints: what not to do (no fluff, don't invent numbers, don't answer off-topic).
s2.validate: Your instruction contains all four blocks: role, style, format, constraints.
s2.tip: Don't duplicate personal facts about yourself here — that's what Custom Instructions are for.

s3.title: Removing vagueness
s3.why: Claude can't act on generic words: "be helpful" sets neither a role nor a format. Specificity is the only thing that actually changes answers.
instructions: Go through each phrase and ask: can I verify this in the answer? If not — the phrase is too generic.
Replace judgment words with measurable rules: "write concisely" → "no more than 5 points".
Add domain context to the role, not just a job title.
Delete anything that doesn't affect the answer: polite wishes and motivation are ignored by Claude.
s3.validate: No phrases remain in the instruction that can't be checked against the answer text.
s3.tip: Vagueness test: if a phrase could be pasted into anyone else's project unchanged — it's too generic.

s4.title: Example and template
s4.why: A ready skeleton saves time and keeps you from forgetting any of the four blocks. It's reusable in new projects.
instructions: Study the example: "You're an expert in my domain. Answer structure: Context → Problem → Impact → Recommendation. English only. No generic phrases, rely on project files".
Take the template: "Role: … / Style: … / Format: … / Don't: …".
Fill each line for your task, keeping the wording concrete.
Save the template separately — it'll help when creating your next project.
s4.validate: You have a filled four-line template for a specific project.
s4.tip: Start with a short instruction and expand it as you notice recurring edits.

s5.title: Test: does the instruction work?
s5.why: An instruction is useless if answers didn't change. A quick test shows whether it's actually being read.
instructions: Ask the same question in the project with the instruction and in a plain chat without it.
Compare the role, format, and language of the answers — the difference is the instruction's effect.
Ask directly: "What instructions are you answering by right now?" and check against what you wrote.
If the answer ignores a rule — the wording is too soft; rewrite it harder and more concretely.
s5.validate: The answer in the project clearly differs from the answer in a clean chat and matches your instruction.
s5.tip: Test after every major change to the instruction — that's how you instantly see what worked.

s6.title: Maintenance and the link to files
s6.why: A project lives and changes, and a stale instruction quietly spoils answers. Linking to files frees the instruction from extra detail.
instructions: Reread the instruction periodically: the project's role may have shifted.
Keep factual material (terms, data, examples) not in the instruction but in [[node:p-files|project files]] — the instruction only sets behavior.
Reference the files in the instruction: "rely on the project materials", instead of copying their content.
Look into [[node:i-project|project instructions]] to bring role, files, and format into one system.
s6.validate: The instruction describes behavior, while facts are moved to project files; the two parts don't duplicate each other.
s6.tip: If the instruction grows too large — move the reference part into files and leave only behavior rules in the field.

project-team.title: Team work in Projects
project-team.subtitle: Shared context instead of scattered chats — for Team and Enterprise
project-team.whatItIs:
On Team and Enterprise plans a [[node:projects|Project]] can be shared with the whole team: people don't each work with their own Claude, but with one shared context — shared [[node:p-instructions|instructions]], [[node:p-files|files]] and agreements.

The result is a single quality standard and one source of truth. A newcomer opens the shared Project and immediately sees the working context instead of piecing it together from colleagues' chats. This course shows how to set up such a shared Project and keep it in good shape.
project-team.approach: Core principle: one Project = one shared source of truth for the team. Don't spin up a project per person. Decide in advance who is responsible for instructions and files and who just uses them. You change access and invite people yourself in the interface — Claude doesn't do it for you.
outcomes: You understand why a team needs a shared Project instead of personal chats
You know the requirements: a Team/Enterprise plan and member roles
You can share a Project and invite the team through the interface
You know what to put in shared context: instructions, files, agreements
You keep hygiene: a single source of truth and clear ownership

applyIn.title: Newcomer onboarding
applyIn.description: A person opens the shared Project and immediately gets the working context — no need to forward a dozen chats.

applyIn.title: Team quality standard
applyIn.description: The design system, brand tone, and code rules live in one Project — everyone answers equally consistently.

applyIn.title: Handover during leave or departure
applyIn.description: Knowledge lives in the shared Project, not in one person's head — work doesn't stall.

pitfalls: Creating a separate Project per person — the point of shared context is lost.
Letting everyone change instructions without review — the project drifts in an unexpected direction.
Leaving stale files in shared context — the team works from outdated knowledge.
Blurry ownership: it's unclear who updates the knowledge, so nobody does.
Duplicates: two similar Projects on one topic — people get confused about where the truth is.

exercises.question: Name one process in your team where people currently work each in their own chat. Describe what would go into a shared Project: instructions, files, agreements.
exercises.hint: A good candidate is where everyone does similar work and consistency of the result matters.

exercises.question: Decide who on the team will be the "knowledge owner" of the shared Project — who updates instructions and files. State a simple rule for how changes are made.
exercises.hint: One owner plus a "change via a short review" rule is enough to avoid chaos.

exercises.question: Check your plan in account settings. Is Project sharing available to you? If not, which plan do you need?
exercises.hint: Project sharing is available on Team and Enterprise plans, not on personal Free/Pro.

s1.title: Why a team needs a shared Project
s1.why: When everyone has their own Claude and their own chats, knowledge breaks into pieces: one set the tone, another uploaded the needed files, a third keeps the rules in their head. A shared [[node:projects|Project]] gathers this into one context — and the team answers to a single standard.
instructions: Recall a process where several people do similar work: product department, design team, support.
Note where knowledge is currently scattered — personal chats, threads, files on different drives.
State the value of a shared Project in one phrase: shared context instead of scattered chats.
Estimate the effect: a newcomer gets up to speed far faster when the context already lives in the project.
s1.validate: You can name a specific team process that would benefit from shared context.
s1.tip: Start with one process, not the whole team at once. One successful shared Project convinces better than any explanation.

s2.title: Requirements: plan and roles
s2.why: Project sharing is a Team and Enterprise feature. On personal Free and Pro there is no shared Project. Before setup it's worth understanding roles too: who administers, who edits the knowledge, who just uses it.
instructions: Open account settings and check your current plan: personal (Free/Pro) or team (Team/Enterprise).
If there's no Team/Enterprise plan — discuss the move with whoever manages the team's subscription.
Map the roles: who owns/admins the workspace, who is responsible for the Project content, who is a member.
Agree that changing [[node:p-instructions|instructions]] and [[node:p-files|files]] is for the responsible people, not everyone.
s2.validate: You know your plan and understand which roles people will have in the shared Project.
s2.tip: Roles aren't just technical. Even if the interface lets everyone do everything, the agreement on "who changes what" matters more than settings.

s3.title: Share the Project and invite the team
s3.why: For the context to become shared, the Project must be opened to the team and members invited. You do this yourself in the interface — via the Share button. Claude does not manage access for you.
instructions: Open the relevant [[node:projects|Project]] and find the Share button.
Choose yourself who gets access: the whole team workspace or specific people.
Invite the members yourself and set their access level according to the roles from step 2.
Verify the result: open the Project as another member (or ask a colleague) and confirm access works as intended.
s3.validate: The team can see the shared Project, and access levels match the roles.
s3.tip: Change access deliberately. If you're unsure whether to give someone edit access — start with view and expand later.

s4.title: What to put in shared context
s4.why: A shared Project's value is in what's inside it. Useful context is [[node:p-instructions|instructions]] (how to answer, tone, format), [[node:p-files|files]] (documents, guidelines, examples) and recorded team agreements.
instructions: In the Project instructions write the shared standard: role, tone, answer format, important constraints.
Upload to files what the team turns to constantly: guidelines, templates, references.
Record agreements in text: what counts as "done", which terms to use and how.
Remove clutter: only current, team-wide material belongs in shared context, not personal drafts.
s4.validate: The shared Project holds instructions, the needed files, and clear agreements — no junk.
s4.tip: Write instructions as if explaining to a new colleague on day one. If they'd understand it, Claude will too.

s5.title: Hygiene of collaboration
s5.why: Shared context is valuable as long as it's current and has one owner. Without rules it quickly turns into a dump: stale files, contradictory instructions, nobody knowing where the truth is.
instructions: Assign an owner of the Project knowledge — who updates instructions and files.
Introduce a change rule: edits to shared context go through a short review, not silently.
Keep a single source of truth: one topic — one Project, no parallel copies.
Periodically review the files: flag or remove the outdated, add the new.
Record important changes in text so the team understands what changed and why.
s5.validate: The shared Project has a knowledge owner, a change rule, and a single source of truth.
s5.tip: A simple "one owns it, others propose" rule prevents chaos better than any elaborate procedure.

s6.title: Common problems and how to avoid them
s6.why: Team Projects break in predictable ways: duplicates, stale knowledge, blurry ownership, and uncontrolled edits to instructions. Knowing the traps in advance makes them easy to avoid.
instructions: Duplicates: before creating a new Project, check there isn't a similar one already — otherwise the team splits.
Stale knowledge: build the habit of periodically reviewing files and instructions for relevance.
Blurry ownership: there is always one knowledge owner — otherwise nobody updates it.
Uncontrolled edits: the responsible people change [[node:p-instructions|instructions]]; others propose via review.
Too-broad access: grant edit access deliberately, by role, not to everyone.
s6.validate: You know four typical traps of shared Projects and your rule against each.
s6.tip: Most problems aren't technical, they're about agreements. First agree on "who's responsible for what", then configure access.

project-when.title: When to create a Project vs. just use Chat
project-when.subtitle: The "time for a Project" signal, anti-patterns, and the first step
project-when.whatItIs: A short decision course: how to tell that a task has outgrown another Chat and deserves a [[node:projects|Project]]. The main signal — a task recurs ≥ 3 times with similar context. You learn to separate one-off from recurring, run a mini-inventory of your scenarios, and avoid spawning needless projects.
project-when.approach: We move from signal to decision: first spot the repetition, then compare Chat and Project for a specific task, run a mini-inventory of your recurring scenarios, separate stable context from one-off, catch the anti-patterns, and finally decide and put the first things into the Project — [[node:p-instructions|instructions]] and [[node:p-files|files]].
outcomes: Learn the "time for a Project" signal: a task recurs ≥ 3 times with similar context
Choose between a regular Chat and a Project deliberately, per task
Run a mini-inventory of your recurring scenarios
Separate stable context (into a Project) from one-off (into Chat)
Recognize anti-patterns: a Project for a single task, a swarm of tiny projects

applyIn.title: A recurring work theme
applyIn.description: One client, product, or line of work you return to for weeks — a candidate for a Project with stable context.

applyIn.title: A one-off question
applyIn.description: Ask something quickly, parse a single document, sketch an idea — stay in a regular Chat, no overhead.

applyIn.title: Cleaning up
applyIn.description: Too many chats piled up on one topic — gather them into a single Project and stop repeating context every time.

pitfalls: Creating a Project for a one-off task — overkill, a regular chat is enough.
Spinning up a dozen tiny projects "just in case" — later you can't remember what's where.
Putting off a Project even though you're retelling the same context by hand for the fifth time.
Dumping unrelated topics into one Project — context blurs and answers lose precision.
Creating a Project and leaving it empty — without instructions and files it's just a chat with an extra name.

exercises.question: Recall the past week: which task did you give Claude ≥ 3 times with a similar intro? Write it down in one line.
exercises.hint: The tell-tale sign — each time you re-explain who you are, what you're working on, and the format you need.

exercises.question: Take that task and decide: Project or Chat? Name one argument for your decision.
exercises.hint: Repetition + similar context → Project. One-off → Chat. In doubt — it's still a Chat.

exercises.question: For the chosen task, list what is stable in it (repeats every time) versus what changes from request to request.
exercises.hint: The stable parts go into the Project's [[node:p-instructions|instructions]] and [[node:p-files|files]]; the changing parts go into the text of a specific request.

s1.title: Catch the "time for a Project" signal
s1.why: If a task recurs ≥ 3 times with similar context — that's a signal to create a Project. Earlier is premature; later means you've already overpaid the "briefing tax".
instructions: Look at your last week of conversations with Claude.
Mark the tasks that repeated: same topic, same type of request.
Check the context: are you re-explaining the same intro every time (who you are, what you work on, the format you need)?
If both repetition and similar context line up, and it happened ≥ 3 times — the signal has fired.
s1.validate: You can name at least one task that crossed the "≥ 3 times + similar context" threshold.
s1.tip: Don't wait for the tenth time. Three repetitions is already the break-even point for a Project.

s2.title: Chat or Project: what to choose per task
s2.why: Both are valid modes. A Project removes the "briefing tax" and holds context; a regular Chat is faster for one-offs. The right choice saves both time and tokens.
instructions: Chat: a one-off question, an experiment, a quick parse of a single document. Context need not be kept for long.
Project: a long line of work (product, client, research topic) where context is stable and you return to it regularly.
Rule: if you'll have to repeat the context again — it's a Project. If the task closes in one conversation — it's a Chat.
Match your task from step 1 against these two descriptions and pick a mode.
s2.validate: For your task you've chosen Chat or Project and can explain the choice in one sentence.
s2.tip: Project ROI is visible after just 2-3 conversations. If the repetition is obvious, don't delay the decision.

s3.title: Inventory your recurring scenarios
s3.why: The signal from step 1 is rarely the only one. A mini-inventory shows the real picture: where there's repetition and where it's just chance — so you don't create a Project blindly.
instructions: List 5-7 typical tasks you come to Claude with.
Next to each, mark the frequency: one-off / sometimes / regular.
For the regular ones, check context similarity — is the intro really the same each time.
Mark those that passed both filters: frequency "regular" + similar context.
s3.validate: You have a short list of tasks, and each is marked as a Project candidate or not.
s3.tip: Build the list honestly, from the facts of recent weeks — not from what "sometimes happens".

s4.title: What to move into a Project vs. keep in Chat
s4.why: A Project is valuable for stable context that doesn't change from request to request. Mixing stable with one-off blurs the context and answers lose precision.
instructions: For the candidate task, split everything into two columns: "repeats every time" and "changes from request to request".
The stable parts (who you are, rules, format, permanent materials) are the Project's contents: [[node:p-instructions|instructions]] and [[node:p-files|files]].
The changing parts (the specific question, a new chunk of text to review) stay in the text of an individual request inside the Project.
One-off tasks unrelated to this line of work belong in a regular Chat — don't drag them into the Project.
s4.validate: You can show exactly what goes into the Project (stable) and what stays one-off in Chat.
s4.tip: A good test: if something changes every time — it's not Project context, it's part of a specific request.

s5.title: Anti-patterns: when a Project is unnecessary
s5.why: A Project isn't free in attention: each one has to be kept in mind and maintained. Surplus projects create chaos instead of order.
instructions: Anti-pattern 1: a Project for a single one-off task — overkill, a regular chat would have done.
Anti-pattern 2: a swarm of tiny projects "just in case" — later you can't remember what's where.
Anti-pattern 3: one Project for unrelated topics — context blurs and answers lose precision.
Review your list from step 3: are there candidates that actually fall into these traps?
s5.validate: You've reviewed the candidates and removed those that fit the anti-patterns.
s5.tip: Rule of thumb: better one living Project than five abandoned ones.

s6.title: Decision and first step
s6.why: A course is useless without action. The final step turns analysis into a concrete decision: create a Project or not — and what to fill it with right away so it doesn't stay empty.
instructions: Make the call on your main task: Project or Chat.
If Chat — you close the course; you already know the signal and will return when the repetition grows.
If Project — create a [[node:projects|Project]] and put the stable context from step 4 into it straight away.
First, fill in the [[node:p-instructions|instructions]] (who you are, rules, format) and upload the permanent [[node:p-files|files]].
From there, add new materials to this Project as you work — it will grow along with the task.
s6.validate: You either have a deliberate "staying in Chat" or a created Project with filled-in instructions and at least one file.
s6.tip: Creating a Project for my regular task — I'll upload new materials there for review. That's the working cycle.

prompt-4d.title: The 4D Framework: a meta-approach to prompting
prompt-4d.subtitle: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence — four skills that work with any model
prompt-4d.whatItIs: The 4D Framework is Anthropic's meta-framework (co-developed with Ringling College and University College Cork): four skills that apply to any AI interaction regardless of model or tool — Delegation (choosing what to give AI), Description (writing clear prompts), Discernment (evaluating output critically), Diligence (iterating until the result is reliable). Behind the four D's sit 24 specific behaviors of effective AI use.
prompt-4d.approach: This course treats 4D not as theory but as a working checklist. First you'll see why most AI failures are a failure of one of four stages, not of the model. Then you'll master each D in turn with examples, apply the framework to your own task, walk through an end-to-end example from delegation to finished result, and lock in the common mistakes with a self-check.
outcomes: Understand that 4D is a transferable skill, not a trick for one specific model
Tell the four stages apart and pinpoint exactly where your result broke down
Apply 4D as a 30-second checklist before any significant AI task
Delegate only suitable work to AI and keep judgment-heavy decisions for yourself
Drive results through feedback loops instead of shipping the first draft

applyIn.title: Synthesis and analysis of materials
applyIn.description: Distilling several articles, reports or interviews into themes and conclusions: 4D helps decide what to give AI, describe the format precisely, and verify facts before use.

applyIn.title: Work and business communication
applyIn.description: Emails, replies, documents: Delegation flags where human sensitivity is needed, while Discernment and Diligence guard against publishing unverified text.

applyIn.title: Recurring AI tasks in a team
applyIn.description: A shared 4D vocabulary gives the team a common quality checklist: which stage went wrong and how to fix it, without arguing that 'the model is bad'.

pitfalls: Skipping Delegation — giving AI a task that requires human judgment (ethical decisions, sensitive communications)
Skipping Description — giving the right task with a vague prompt and getting a generic, useless answer
Skipping Discernment — accepting hallucinated or unverifiable output as fact
Stopping at one iteration — Diligence means feedback loops, not a single send
Treating 4D as a trick for one model — in reality the skills transfer across all AI tools and don't become obsolete

exercises.question: Take a recent case where AI gave a poor result. Which of the four D's broke down — Delegation, Description, Discernment, or Diligence?
exercises.hint: Ask in order: was the task suitable for AI at all; was the prompt specific; did you verify the output; did you stop at the first draft. The first 'no' is the broken stage.

exercises.question: For your current task, write one sentence for each D.
exercises.hint: Model it on Anthropic's example: Delegation — 'this synthesis is suitable for AI'; Description — 'summarize 5 articles into 3 themes, max 200 words'; Discernment — 'flag the unverifiable statistic'; Diligence — 'revise theme 2, it misses the angle from article 3'.

exercises.question: Turn 4D into a personal 30-second checklist of four questions you'll ask yourself before every significant task.
exercises.hint: Am I delegating the right work? Is my prompt specific enough? Did I verify the output? Is this iteration ready to use?

s1.title: What 4D is and why you need it
s1.why: Without a shared framework, AI failures feel random and get blamed on 'a bad model'. 4D shows that almost every failure happens at one of four manageable stages — which means it can be fixed.
instructions: Read that 4D is four skills — Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence — that apply to any AI tool.
Internalize the key idea: most failures are a failure of a stage, not the model. A strong prompt for the wrong task still gives a poor result.
Remember the skills are transferable: they don't become obsolete when models change, unlike version-specific tricks.
Connect 4D to the fundamentals: it is a meta-level above the specific techniques in [[node:prompting|prompting]] and [[node:pr-principles|good prompt principles]].
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence why 4D is a transferable skill rather than a trick for a specific model.
s1.tip: Keep the split in mind: the model is the tool, 4D is your process for working with the tool. It's usually the process that gets fixed.

s2.title: Delegation and Description: what to give AI and how to describe it
s2.why: The first two D's define the input. A mistake here makes any further effort pointless: the wrong task or a vague prompt guarantees a weak result before generation even starts.
instructions: Delegation: learn to separate tasks suitable for AI (synthesis, drafts, exploring options) from tasks needing human judgment (ethics, sensitive decisions).
Description: state the task concretely — role, format, length, audience. Compare 'summarize the articles' with 'summarize 5 articles into 3 themes for a non-technical audience, max 200 words'.
Strengthen Description with techniques: set a role via [[node:pr-role|role prompting]] and structure complex input via [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]].
Check both D's together: is this the right work for AI, and have I described it precisely enough.
s2.validate: You can use an example to explain the difference between bad Delegation (wrong task) and bad Description (vague prompt).
s2.tip: If the output is 'generic and watery', Description is almost always the culprit, not the model. Add format, length and audience.

s3.title: Discernment and Diligence: evaluating and finishing the result
s3.why: The third and fourth D's define the output. The most expensive mistakes are born here: accepting a hallucination as fact and publishing an unverified first draft.
instructions: Discernment: read the output critically — flag claims and statistics you cannot verify, and don't take them on faith.
Distinguish the AI's confident tone from accuracy: model confidence does not equal correctness.
Diligence: treat the first answer as a draft — give targeted feedback and iterate rather than sending it straight out.
Connect Discernment to transparent reasoning: [[node:pr-cot|chain-of-thought]] helps you see how the AI reached its conclusion and catch errors more easily.
s3.validate: You can name one concrete action for Discernment (what to verify) and one for Diligence (how to improve) on your own example.
s3.tip: Rule of thumb: nothing that comes out of AI goes outside without at least one fact-check and one editing iteration.

s4.title: Applying 4D to your own task
s4.why: The framework only works once it becomes a habit. Applying it to your own real task turns theory into a skill you use automatically.
instructions: Take a concrete task from your work that you plan to give to AI.
Run it through the four D's in turn: write one sentence each for Delegation, Description, Discernment and Diligence.
Turn the questions into a 30-second checklist: am I delegating the right work, is the prompt specific, did I verify the output, is the iteration ready.
Note which of the four stages you usually rush — that is your risk zone.
s4.validate: You have a completed 4D checklist for a real task and know which D you most often skip.
s4.tip: The checklist takes 30 seconds and saves hours of rework. Checking the input and output is cheaper than redoing everything.

s5.title: End-to-end example: from delegation to finished result
s5.why: Seeing 4D in action across one continuous example matters more than knowing the definitions separately: it shows how the stages connect into a loop.
instructions: Delegation — decide: 'synthesizing five research articles is suitable for AI; the final decision stays with me'.
Description — phrase it: 'summarize these 5 articles into 3 key themes for a non-technical audience, max 200 words per theme'.
Discernment — evaluate the output: 'Claude cited a statistic I cannot verify — flag it and don't use it as fact'.
Diligence — iterate: 'revise theme 2, it misses the regulatory angle from article 3', and repeat until the result is reliable.
s5.validate: You can reproduce this loop on your own task, saying all four steps out loud as one process.
s5.tip: Notice: Diligence loops back to Description — a good edit is a new, small, precise prompt.

s6.title: Common mistakes and a final check
s6.why: Knowing the framework and avoiding the usual traps are different things. This step locks in 4D through anti-patterns and self-checking.
instructions: Delegation: don't give AI tasks that require human judgment — ethical decisions and sensitive communications stay with you.
Discernment: don't publish AI output without fact-checking, however convincing it looks.
Diligence: don't stop at one iteration — it's about feedback loops, not a single send.
Run a final self-check: take your last AI result, run all four D's, and find at least one stage you could have done better.
s6.validate: You can list one mistake for each of the four D's and apply the 4D checklist by default before significant tasks.
s6.tip: If it's hard to remember, post the four questions where you can see them. After a couple of weeks they become automatic.

prompt-principles.title: Core Prompt Principles
prompt-principles.subtitle: Context → Role → Task → Format → Constraints — the framework that works almost always
prompt-principles.whatItIs:
Five elements that turn a vague request into a precise one: context (what's the situation), role (who the model should be), task (what exactly to do), format (how to deliver), and constraints (what to avoid). It's not "prompt magic" but a simple habit: 30 seconds of structure save 15 minutes of back-and-forth.

The course walks through each principle in turn with live examples, and at the end you assemble everything into one working prompt and test it. Related nodes: [[node:prompting|prompting]] as the overall discipline, [[node:pr-role|role]], [[node:pr-4d|4D task]], and [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]] for format.
prompt-principles.approach: Don't memorize — apply it right away to your real task. After each step, add one more element to your own prompt, and at the end send it to Claude and compare it with what you'd get without structure.
outcomes: You understand why structure yields an answer you don't have to rewrite
You can set context so the model doesn't have to guess
You assign role and format deliberately, not at random
You phrase the task as one clear action instead of a vague wish
You assemble a full prompt from five blocks in a minute

applyIn.title: Work emails and texts
applyIn.description: Any draft of an email, post, or report goes through the framework — and comes out ready on the first try, not after three rounds of edits.

applyIn.title: Analysis and decisions
applyIn.description: When you need solution options or data analysis, an expert role plus a table format gives a structured, comparable answer.

applyIn.title: Training the team
applyIn.description: The same framework is a shared language for the whole team: prompts become repeatable and easy to hand off.

pitfalls: Writing the task right away without context and role — the model guesses and errs more often.
Specifying format as "make it nicer" instead of specifics ("table: columns A, B, C").
Overloading with constraints — keep 2–3 that truly matter.
Confusing role with task: "be a marketer" is a role, "write 5 headlines" is a task.
Assuming one perfect prompt solves everything — structure sets the foundation, then refine iteratively.

exercises.question: Take your usual one-line request to Claude and add context and a role. Send both versions and compare.
exercises.hint: If there's barely any difference, the context was too generic. Add specifics: who you are, who the result is for.

exercises.question: Phrase the task so it has exactly one action and an explicit output format (list / table / paragraph).
exercises.hint: Check: can you tell unambiguously from your wording what counts as a finished result?

exercises.question: Assemble a full prompt from the five blocks for a real task and run it in Claude.
exercises.hint: If the answer is off, it's almost always one missing block. Find which one.

s1.title: Why structure at all: before and after
s1.why: Until you see the contrast between a vague and a structured request with your own eyes, the principles stay abstract.
instructions: Open Claude and send a short request for a real task, e.g. "Help me with a client email".
Save the answer — this is your "draft without structure".
Don't fix it yet: in the next steps you'll add one element at a time and compare at the end.
Remember the feeling: a generic answer needs clarifications, and each clarification is another round of back-and-forth.
s1.validate: You have one "raw" Claude answer to an unstructured request — a baseline for comparison.
s1.tip: The [[node:prompting|prompting]] framework isn't about length but order. A short but structured prompt almost always beats a long but chaotic one.

s2.title: Context: give the model the picture
s2.why: Without context the model guesses the circumstances and misses more often — and guessing costs you extra edits.
instructions: Add 1–2 sentences to the request: who you are, who the result is for, what the situation is.
Example: "I'm a manager at a B2B service, the client is a month late on payment, and I want to keep the relationship."
Avoid extra detail — only facts that change the answer.
Send the updated request and compare it with the draft from step 1.
s2.validate: The answer is noticeably closer to your situation — the generic "depending on circumstances" phrases are gone.
s2.tip: A good context test: mentally remove it — if the model's answer would change a lot, the context matters and is needed.

s3.title: Role: set the point of view
s3.why: A role tunes the tone, depth, and priorities of the answer: a "lawyer" and a "copywriter" will write the same email very differently.
instructions: Add a role line at the start: "You are an experienced account manager who values long-term client relationships."
Pick a role for the goal, not a "universal expert" — the more precise, the more useful.
Don't confuse role with task: role is "who to be", task is "what to do".
Send it and see how the tone of the answer has shifted.
s3.validate: The tone and emphasis of the answer match the chosen role (e.g. more diplomatic, or conversely firmer).
s3.tip: More on this technique — the [[node:pr-role|role in a prompt]] node: one precise role often replaces a paragraph of instructions.

s4.title: Task: one clear action
s4.why: A vague task ("do it well") gives a vague answer. A clear action verb sets a concrete goal for the model.
instructions: Reframe the essence into one action: "Write an email", "Suggest 3 wording options", "Draft a 5-point plan".
If there are several actions, split them into numbered subtasks rather than piling them up.
Drop the polite "could you possibly" — it doesn't hurt, but the action verb's specificity matters more.
Send the updated prompt.
s4.validate: From the task wording you can unambiguously tell what counts as a finished result.
s4.tip: The task framework is covered in the [[node:pr-4d|4D task]] node: the more concrete the action and scope, the fewer iterations.

s5.title: Format and constraints: how to deliver and what to avoid
s5.why: Format makes the answer ready to use, and constraints cut out what you definitely don't need.
instructions: Specify the format explicitly: "a table with columns Tone / Text / Risk", "a bulleted list", "no longer than 150 words".
Add 2–3 constraints: "no jargon", "don't mention the amount", "tone friendly but firm".
Don't overload — extra constraints contradict each other and confuse the model.
For complex formats use separator tags (see [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]]) so the model doesn't blend blocks.
s5.validate: The answer arrived in exactly the requested format and without what you forbade.
s5.tip: If the format is complex, show the model a 2-line mini-sample. An example beats any description.

s6.title: Assemble it into one prompt and test
s6.why: The power of the framework shows only when all five elements work together — and that's easy to verify by comparison.
instructions: Assemble the final prompt in order: Context → Role → Task → Format → Constraints.
Send it to Claude in a fresh chat — without the history of past attempts.
Compare the result with the "raw" draft from step 1.
If something is off, find the missing or weak block and strengthen just that one instead of rewriting everything.
s6.validate: The final answer is usable with almost no edits and is noticeably better than the draft from step 1.
s6.tip: Save a successful prompt as a template with placeholders — the [[node:prompting|prompting]] framework gets reused across dozens of tasks.

prompt-xml.title: XML tags in prompts for Claude
prompt-xml.subtitle: Mark up your prompts with tags so Claude doesn't confuse data with instructions
prompt-xml.whatItIs: Claude is trained to understand XML-like markup especially well: blocks such as <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>. Tags turn a wall of text into a structure where the model can see where the data is, where the task is, where the example is, and where the constraints are. It's not magic — just explicit signaling of the boundaries between meaningful blocks.
prompt-xml.approach: We move from motivation to practice: first why mark up a prompt at all, then the basic tag set, then marking up a long prompt, a before/after example walkthrough, nesting and referencing tags inside the instruction — and finally common mistakes with a validation checklist. XML tags in this course are kept as-is and never replaced with emoji or markdown.
outcomes: You understand why Claude works more stably with XML markup on long prompts
You use the basic tag set <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>
You can mark up a long prompt so data doesn't blend into instructions
You apply nested tags and reference them in the instruction text
You avoid typical mistakes: extra tags, unclosed blocks, marking up simple requests

applyIn.title: Long prompts with data
applyIn.description: When you paste a large document, log, or code into a prompt, you wrap it in <context> or <data>, and keep the task separately in <task>, so Claude doesn't mistake the data for an instruction.

applyIn.title: Few-shot examples
applyIn.description: You wrap each training example in <example> so the model clearly separates samples from the current request. See [[node:pr-fewshot|learning from examples]].

applyIn.title: Complex tasks with constraints
applyIn.description: When a task has many conditions, you move them into <constraints> so Claude doesn't lose requirements in the general flow of text.

pitfalls: Marking up a simple one-line request with tags — that's noise, not value
Forgetting the closing tag (</task>) — block boundaries blur and the model gets confused
Inventing dozens of exotic tags instead of 3-4 clear ones — the structure stops being readable
Putting data and instruction in one block — the whole point of markup is lost
Referencing a tag in the instruction that isn't in the prompt — Claude can't find what you mean

exercises.question: You have a prompt: a long article text, and at the end the phrase "summarize it". How do you tag it so Claude doesn't confuse the article with the instruction?
exercises.hint: Wrap the article itself in <context>...</context>, and the command in a separate <task>summarize it</task>.

exercises.question: You want to give Claude 3 examples of correct answers and 1 new question. Which tags do you use?
exercises.hint: Each sample goes in its own <example>, the current request in <task>. That way the model sees the examples are training, not data to answer.

exercises.question: Why write "use the data from the <context> tag" in the instruction if the data is already in the prompt?
exercises.hint: An explicit tag reference removes ambiguity: Claude knows exactly which block to treat as the source and which to ignore.

s1.title: Why Claude needs XML markup
s1.why: Without structure, a long prompt is a wall of text where the model guesses where the data ends and the task begins. XML tags give explicit boundaries, and on complex tasks the result becomes 2-3 times more stable.
instructions: Take one of your long prompts where data and instruction run as solid text
Visually mark where the "material" is (text, code, log) and where the "command" is — what to do with it
Recognize the problem: without markup Claude may mistake some data for an instruction or vice versa
Remember the idea: a tag is an explicit signal "a separate meaningful block starts here"
Connect this to the basics in [[node:prompting|prompting]] — XML is a structure tool, not a replacement for a clear request
s1.validate: You can explain in one sentence what problem XML markup solves (separating data from instructions).
s1.tip: XML tags in Claude don't have to be "real" valid XML — what matters is a clear pairing of opening and closing tag.

s2.title: Basic tags: <context>, <task>, <example>, <constraints>
s2.why: You don't need to invent your own notation. Four tags cover 90% of tasks, and they're intuitive both to you and the model.
instructions: <context> — put background information, data, a document, or code here
<task> — one clear statement of what needs to be done
<example> — samples of the desired answer, one example per tag
<constraints> — limits: format, length, tone, what to avoid
Remember: tag names in lowercase, every opened tag is closed (</task>)
s2.validate: You can name the purpose of each of the four basic tags without a hint.
s2.tip: A tag name should describe its content: <context>, <data>, <transcript> are better than faceless <block1>, <block2>.

s3.title: How to mark up a long prompt
s3.why: The main benefit of markup shows up precisely on long prompts: when there's a lot of material, without tags the model loses track of what's the source and what's the task.
instructions: Split the prompt into meaningful parts: background, data, task, constraints, examples
Wrap each part in a suitable tag and close it
Place <task> closer to the end — that keeps the instruction "fresh" in context
Never put data and command in one block — those are different tags
Lean on the principles from [[node:pr-principles|prompting principles]]: one task = one clear statement
s3.validate: Your long prompt is split into at least 3 tags, and each block contains only one type of content.
s3.tip: The order "context → data → task → constraints" works best: the model gets the background first, then the command.

s4.title: A worked example: before and after
s4.why: The contrast between "flat text" and a "marked-up prompt" shows what XML structure actually gives you more vividly than any theory.
instructions: BEFORE (flat): "Here's an article about coffee ... at the end make a short summary in 3 points, no fluff"
AFTER: <context>text of the article about coffee...</context>
Add the task separately: <task>make a short summary of the article</task>
Add constraints: <constraints>3 points, no fluff, in English</constraints>
Compare: in the AFTER version Claude knows for sure the article is the source, not part of the instruction
s4.validate: You rewrote one of your real "flat" prompts into a marked-up version with at least three tags.
s4.tip: If the result improved, save the marked-up template and reuse it, changing only the contents of <context>.

s5.title: Nesting and referencing tags in the instruction
s5.why: When structure gets more complex, tags can be nested, and the instruction can explicitly reference them by name. This removes the last bit of ambiguity.
instructions: Nest tags when there's a hierarchy: <examples><example>...</example><example>...</example></examples>
Don't overdo depth — two levels of nesting are almost always enough
In the task text reference a tag by name: "use the data from <context>, take the format from <example>"
That way Claude knows exactly which block is the source and which is the sample
For structured output, connect with [[node:pr-structured|structured output]] — ask for the answer in tags too, e.g. <answer>
s5.validate: You wrote an instruction that references at least one tag from the prompt by name.
s5.tip: Asking to "return the answer inside <answer>...</answer>" makes later automatic parsing of the result easier.

s6.title: Common mistakes and validation
s6.why: XML markup breaks on small things: an unclosed tag, extra markup on a simple request, a reference to a nonexistent block. A final checklist catches this before you send.
instructions: Check pairing: every <tag> has a closing </tag>
Remove markup if the request is short and unambiguous — there tags are noise
Make sure data and instruction sit in different tags, not one
Check that all tags referenced by the instruction actually exist in the prompt
Run the prompt and look: did Claude take the data from where you expected?
s6.validate: You went through the 4-point checklist on your prompt and found no unclosed or extra tags.
s6.tip: Not sure if markup is needed? The rule is simple: a long prompt with different data types — yes; a short question — no.

prompt-fewshot.title: Few-shot: teaching by input→output examples
prompt-fewshot.subtitle: Show 1-3 examples — and the model picks up the pattern without long explanations
prompt-fewshot.whatItIs:
Few-shot is a technique where instead of describing a task in words, you show ready input→output pairs. The model picks up the pattern from the examples and continues it on new data. It is the strongest way to lock in a format, tone, and style that are hard to put into instructions.

Where zero-shot (just an instruction) gives a vague result, two or three precise examples set a firm frame. Few-shot pairs well with [[node:prompting|basic prompting]] and [[node:pr-xml|XML structure]], which cleanly separates the examples from the request.
prompt-fewshot.approach: Don't explain what's easier to show. Give 1-3 diverse, non-contradictory examples in a single format, wrap them in tags, and end with a real input without an answer — the model will complete the output by pattern. Example quality matters more than quantity.
outcomes: Understand when examples beat verbal instructions
Choose the right number of examples (1-3) and their diversity
Format input→output pairs via XML tags so the model doesn't confuse them with the request
Recognize and remove example bias and contradictions
Combine few-shot with other techniques and validate the result

applyIn.title: Non-standard output format
applyIn.description: When you need a specific JSON, table, or markup that's hard to describe in words — show 2 ready examples.

applyIn.title: Subtle tone and style
applyIn.description: When brand voice or a specific intonation matters — examples convey it more precisely than any description.

applyIn.title: Classification and labeling
applyIn.description: When you need to sort texts into categories — a few labeled examples set the class boundaries.

pitfalls: Contradictory examples — the model picks a random pattern and the result drifts.
Example bias: if all examples are from one category, the model leans toward it even where it shouldn't.
Too many examples (5+) — they bloat the prompt and rarely improve accuracy over 2-3.
Examples not separated from the request — the model confuses 'samples' with 'the task to perform'.
All examples are easy, with no edge cases — the model stumbles on atypical input.

exercises.question: Take a task you usually describe in words (e.g. 'summarize in 3 bullets') and rebuild it as few-shot: give 2 input→output pairs and one new input. Compare the result to the purely verbal version.
exercises.hint: Wrap examples in <example>...</example> tags so the model doesn't mistake them for the task.

exercises.question: Create deliberately contradictory examples (one output in uppercase, another in lowercase) and see which pattern the model picks on a new input.
exercises.hint: The unpredictable answer is a clear demonstration of why examples must be consistent.

exercises.question: Add one edge-case example (empty input, very long text, atypical case) and check whether the result became more robust.
exercises.hint: An edge example shows the model how to behave in exceptions, not just in ideal cases.

s1.title: What few-shot is and when it beats explanations
s1.why: The key insight: showing a finished result is often more effective than describing it. Few-shot removes ambiguity where words fail — in format, tone, and structure.
instructions: State the task two ways: as a verbal instruction (zero-shot) and as an input→output example.
Ask yourself: can you describe the desired format in one precise sentence? If not — that's a signal for few-shot.
Remember the rule: format, tone, and style are almost always better shown; facts and logic are better explained (see [[node:prompting|basic prompting]]).
Few-shot gives roughly +30-80% format accuracy compared to zero-shot.
s1.validate: You can name a concrete task where an example is more precise than any description.
s1.tip: If you catch yourself writing a long paragraph on 'exactly how to format the answer' — almost always it should be replaced by a single example.

s2.title: How many examples (1-3) and which ones
s2.why: The number and diversity of examples directly shape the result. Too few — the model won't catch the pattern; too many — bloat the prompt; too similar — create bias.
instructions: Start with one example (one-shot). If the pattern is unstable — add a second and a third.
Stop at 2-3 examples: beyond that accuracy grows little while prompt length and cost grow noticeably.
Make examples diverse: different inputs, different cases, not three copies of the same thing.
If the task has categories — cover different categories with examples, not just one.
s2.validate: You have 1-3 dissimilar examples covering the typical cases of the task.
s2.tip: Diversity matters more than quantity: two different examples are stronger than five nearly identical ones.

s3.title: How to format examples: input→output pairs and XML
s3.why: The model must clearly understand which parts are samples and which is the actual task. Without markup it confuses examples with the request and tries to 'perform' them.
instructions: Format each example as an explicit pair: input and expected output side by side.
Wrap examples in tags, e.g. <example><input>...</input><output>...</output></example> — this is [[node:pr-xml|XML structure]].
Keep a single format across all examples: same tags, same output structure.
At the end, give a new input without an output — the model will complete the answer by pattern.
Don't mix several output formats in one example.
s3.validate: Examples are visually and structurally separated from the final request, and the format is identical across all.
s3.tip: Uniform tags are half the battle: the model copies exactly the structure it sees in the examples.

s4.title: A worked example
s4.why: One worked case cements everything above: the number of examples, their formatting, and the final input in action.
instructions: Task: extract the sentiment of a review. Give two examples: <example><input>Delivery was a week late</input><output>negative</output></example> and <example><input>Everything arrived on time, packaging perfect</input><output>positive</output></example>.
Add an edge example with a mixed case: <example><input>The product is good, but support is silent</input><output>mixed</output></example>.
At the end, give a new input without an answer: <input>The price stings, but the quality is top-notch</input>.
Run it and check that the model returned a single word from the given set, not a long text.
s4.validate: The model answers strictly in the examples' format (a single label word), including the mixed case.
s4.tip: Including an edge example ('mixed') pre-teaches the model not to fall into binary thinking.

s5.title: Common pitfalls: bias and contradictions
s5.why: Most few-shot failures aren't a lack of examples but their poor quality: contradictions and a skew toward one category.
instructions: Check examples for contradictions: the same input type must not produce different output formats.
Check balance: if all examples are one category — the model will lean toward it (example bias).
Make sure the order and frequency of examples don't artificially hint at the 'right' answer.
Remove duplicate examples — they add no signal, only length.
s5.validate: Examples are mutually consistent and balanced across categories, with no duplicates.
s5.tip: If the result 'jumps' from run to run — contradictory examples are almost always to blame, not the model.

s6.title: Validation and combining with other techniques
s6.why: Few-shot isn't an isolated trick. It's amplified by structure and reasoning, and a final check confirms the pattern was truly picked up.
instructions: Run the prompt on 3-5 new inputs and confirm the format stays stable across all.
Combine few-shot with [[node:pr-xml|XML structure]] for a clean separation of examples and request.
For complex tasks add a [[node:pr-cot|chain of thought]]: let examples show both the reasoning and the final output.
If the format is stable — save the prompt as a reusable template.
s6.validate: The format reproduces stably on new inputs, and the prompt is saved as a ready template.
s6.tip: Few-shot + [[node:pr-cot|chain-of-thought]]: examples that show reasoning teach the model not only the answer format but the way to think.

prompt-cot.title: Chain of Thought: reasoning step by step
prompt-cot.subtitle: Make the model think out loud — and get the right answer on hard tasks
prompt-cot.whatItIs:
Chain of Thought (CoT) is a technique where you ask the model not to blurt out an answer, but to first walk through logical steps: unpack the conditions, weigh the options, check itself — and only then give a conclusion. The model literally "thinks out loud."

Why it works: each reasoning step becomes context for the next one. A complex task breaks into small pieces, and the model stumbles less often. On logic, math, and multi-step analysis, CoT adds +20-40% accuracy compared to answering head-on.

This course teaches not just writing "think step by step," but managing the reasoning: where to turn it on, how to separate it from the final answer, and where it only gets in the way.
prompt-cot.approach: Don't memorize phrases. Take one REAL task where Claude errs or answers shallowly (a calculation, comparing options, analyzing a situation). Run it through every step of the course and watch how the answer changes. By the end you'll have a working prompt with controlled reasoning and an understanding of when CoT isn't needed.
outcomes: Recognize tasks where step-by-step reasoning genuinely raises accuracy
Turn on CoT with the right wording ("think step by step," tag markup)
Separate the draft reasoning from a clean final answer
Avoid wasting tokens and time on CoT where it's unnecessary
Understand how CoT relates to extended thinking mode

applyIn.title: Analysis and comparisons
applyIn.description: Evaluate options, weigh pros and cons, draw a conclusion from conditions — CoT stops the model from cutting corners and giving a shallow opinion.

applyIn.title: Math and calculations
applyIn.description: Multi-stage computations, percentages, conversions. Step-by-step reasoning catches arithmetic errors before they reach the answer.

applyIn.title: Multi-step tasks
applyIn.description: When the answer must be "derived" through 3-5 intermediate inferences rather than recalled as a fact. CoT holds the logic together step to step.

pitfalls: Turning on CoT for simple factual questions — you get a long wall of reasoning for a one-word answer.
Not separating reasoning from the conclusion — the user drowns in the draft and can't find the result.
Asking to "think step by step" but giving no step structure on a hard task — the reasoning becomes vague.
Ignoring token cost: long CoT in every request makes work more expensive and slower.
Confusing CoT with extended thinking — they're different: you set the first with a prompt, the second is a model mode.

exercises.question: Take an analytical task (e.g. "which of three options is best and why") and solve it TWICE: once with a plain prompt, once adding "First analyze each option step by step, then conclude." Compare depth and accuracy.
exercises.hint: The effect is clearer on tasks with several criteria and trade-offs.

exercises.question: Take a CoT prompt and add the requirement: "Put reasoning in <reasoning> tags, give the final answer after them as one paragraph." Check that the result is now clean and readable.
exercises.hint: This way the draft of thinking doesn't interfere with using the finished answer.

exercises.question: Find a simple question ("capital of France," "translate a word"), attach "think step by step" to it, and look at the bloated answer. Note why CoT here is an anti-pattern.
exercises.hint: If the answer is a fact, not a derivation, the reasoning only wastes tokens.

s1.title: Understand what CoT is and when it helps
s1.why: CoT isn't "magic for every request" — it's a tool for tasks where the answer must be derived, not recalled. First learn to tell those tasks apart.
instructions: Remember the essence: CoT is asking the model to reason out loud, step by step, before the final answer.
Write down 3 of your own tasks where Claude answered shallowly or made errors: calculations, comparisons, situation analysis.
Note the sign of a "CoT task": the answer can't be given in one phrase — it must be DERIVED from the conditions.
This is a core prompting technique — see [[node:prompting|prompt engineering]] for the broader context.
Pick ONE task from the list — you'll carry it through the whole course.
s1.validate: You have one real task where the answer must be derived by logic, not recalled as a fact.
s1.tip: Marker test: if you'd solve the task on paper or "by hand," it's a candidate for CoT.

s2.title: Learn how to ask for reasoning
s2.why: The model won't turn on CoT by itself on a short request. You need explicit wording — from a simple trigger to structured steps.
instructions: Simplest way: add "Think step by step before answering" at the end of the prompt.
Stronger: set the step structure — "1) list the data 2) form options 3) check each 4) conclude."
More reliable still: ask to wrap the reasoning in a tag, e.g. "Reason inside <reasoning>...</reasoning>."
Run your task from step 1 with the "think step by step" trigger and save the answer.
Tag markup is an XML-structuring technique — see [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]].
s2.validate: Your answer now contains visible intermediate reasoning steps, not just a conclusion up front.
s2.tip: The harder the task, the more concretely you should set the steps — "think step by step" alone gets vague.

s3.title: Separate reasoning from the final answer
s3.why: Raw reasoning helps the model but hinders the human. The final answer must be separated and readable on its own.
instructions: Ask explicitly: "Put reasoning in <reasoning>, give the final answer after it as a separate block."
Or: "At the end, under the heading SUMMARY, give a clean answer with no reasoning."
Check: can you copy just the final block and use it without the draft.
If the result is still "smeared" across the reasoning, strengthen the instruction: "Summary — max 3 sentences."
Tagging the reasoning relies on [[node:pr-xml|XML tags]] for block boundaries.
s3.validate: The answer clearly shows two blocks: reasoning and a separate clean summary usable on its own.
s3.tip: The final answer should make sense to someone who did NOT read the reasoning — that's the test of good separation.

s4.title: Work through a detailed example
s4.why: Theory sticks on a full example. Walk a task end to end — from conditions to a clean conclusion — and see the technique at work.
instructions: Take the task: "A team has 3 tools (A — $20/mo, B — $35/mo, C — free but weaker). Budget is $50, integrations and support are needed. Which to choose?"
Prompt: "Solve step by step in <reasoning>: 1) list criteria 2) rate each tool 3) match against budget 4) conclude. Then under the heading RECOMMENDATION — a clean answer."
Watch how the model, in reasoning, runs through the options, catches the budget constraint, and justifies the choice.
Compare: the same question without CoT usually gives "take B, it's popular" — with no criteria analysis.
Transfer this structure to your own task from step 1.
s4.validate: You see how step-by-step reasoning leads to a justified conclusion, and you've repeated the structure on your task.
s4.tip: A good CoT example always shows WHY alternatives were rejected, not just what was chosen.

s5.title: Understand when CoT is unnecessary
s5.why: CoT costs tokens and time. On simple tasks it doesn't raise accuracy, only bloats the answer. Knowing the boundary matters.
instructions: Don't apply CoT to factual questions ("capital of...," "translate a word," "release date") — the answer is recalled, not derived.
Don't apply it to simple single-step tasks — the reasoning there is longer than the answer itself.
Mind the cost: long CoT in every request is more expensive and slower, especially at scale.
For genuinely hard tasks there's a separate mode — [[node:cap-thinking|extended thinking]], where the model thinks longer without a manual CoT prompt.
Distinguish: you set CoT in words in the prompt; extended thinking is a model mode enabled by a setting.
s5.validate: You can explain with an example why CoT on a simple question is an anti-pattern, and you know about extended thinking as an alternative.
s5.tip: Rule: no derivation from conditions, no CoT. A fact or a single operation — answer directly.

s6.title: Verify the result
s6.why: A final check cements the skill: you should be able both to turn CoT on where it's needed and off where it isn't.
instructions: Take your task from step 1 and confirm: the answer with CoT is more accurate and better justified than without it.
Check that the final summary is separated and readable without the reasoning draft.
Take a simple question and confirm you do NOT force CoT onto it.
Formulate a one-line rule for yourself: "when I turn on step-by-step reasoning."
Save the working prompt template with the <reasoning> tag to your notes for reuse.
s6.validate: You have a ready CoT prompt template and a clear rule for which tasks to apply it to and which not.
s6.tip: The best check is to give your final answer to a colleague: did they grasp the conclusion without reading the reasoning?

prompt-role.title: Role and context
