applyIn.description: The server reaches your databases and services. A clean tools surface cuts wrong calls and makes it easier for colleagues to maintain.

applyIn.title: Public or client MCP server
applyIn.description: External users connect your server to Claude. Meaningful names and reliable responses decide whether it feels handy or annoying.

applyIn.title: Refactoring an overgrown server
applyIn.description: The server has sprawled into dozens of tools and universal combine-harvesters. You apply patterns to shrink and sharpen the surface.

pitfalls: A "universal tool" with ten parameters and an action field — the model gets lost in the combinations
Technical names like exec1 or doStuff — Claude can't tell when to call them
Silent errors or raw stack traces instead of a clear message — the model can't recover
Lists without pagination — a huge response floods the context and kills usefulness
Everything modeled as a tool, even static references that should be resources

exercises.question: You have a tool manage_user(action, id, data) where action is create/read/update/delete. Why is this an anti-pattern and how would you redo it?
exercises.hint: Think about how the model picks the action value and how to describe side effects. Compare with the read/write split from [[node:mcp|MCP]].

exercises.question: The tool list_orders returns all orders of all time in a single array. What two changes make the response reliable?
exercises.hint: One is about response size and context, the other about predictable structure on error.

exercises.question: You need to expose a country-code reference to Claude that changes once a year. Tool or resource? Justify it.
exercises.hint: Compare: a tool is called with arguments and may have side effects; a resource is readable data at an address.

s1.title: Why design patterns
s1.why: Tool-call quality depends not on the model's power but on how easily it can grasp your surface. Bad design forces Claude to guess — and to err.
instructions: Remember the core principle: the model should be able to call a tool easily and correctly using only its name, description and schema
State the server's purpose in one sentence — it's a filter for future decisions
Look at your (or someone's) server through the model's eyes: is it clear without docs what to call when
Fix a success metric: fewer wrong and redundant tool calls, not more functions
s1.validate: You can name the server's purpose in one sentence and explain why good design reduces tool-choice errors.
s1.tip: Good patterns yield 3-5x fewer tool-choice errors from Claude — that pays back the design time. Protocol basics are in [[node:mcp|MCP]].

s2.title: Minimal tools surface
s2.why: The fewer and sharper the tools, the more confidently the model picks the right one. Broad combine-harvesters with many parameters confuse Claude more than a few narrow tools.
instructions: List every needed operation and group them by meaning
Replace universal tools with an action field with separate narrow tools per operation
Remove tools that duplicate each other or are barely used
Separate reads and writes: get_users (read) apart from delete_user (write)
Check that each tool has the minimal sufficient parameter set, with no optional "just in case" fields
s2.validate: The server has no tool with an action field or ten parameters, and read and write operations are split apart.
s2.tip: Rule: better 3 narrow tools than one broad one. A narrow tool is easier to describe and nearly impossible to call out of place.

s3.title: Meaningful names, descriptions and schemas
s3.why: The model picks a tool by its name, description and parameter schema — that's its only source of truth. Vague names and empty descriptions turn the choice into guesswork.
instructions: Give each tool a verb name reflecting the action: get_orders, create_invoice, not data1 or handler
In the description say what the tool does, when to use it and whether it has side effects
For each parameter set a clear name, type and short explanation; mark the required ones
Explicitly flag destructive actions (delete, write) and describe what will happen
Use a single namespace and naming style across the server so tools read as one family
s3.validate: From any tool's name and description you can tell, without code, what it does, when it's needed and what it changes.
s3.tip: A tool's description is a prompt for the model. Write it as if explaining to a colleague seeing the tool for the first time. Custom-server details are in [[node:m-custom|Your own MCP server]].

s4.title: Response format and reliability
s4.why: The model builds its next steps on the tool's response. A predictable structure, clear errors and pagination let Claude recover and avoid clogging the context with junk.
instructions: Make the successful-response structure stable and identical across similar tools
Return errors as clear text with a cause and a hint on what to do, not a raw stack trace
For lists add pagination (limit, cursor) and don't hand back everything in one giant array
Return only the needed fields — extra data bloats the context and lowers accuracy
Make write operations idempotent where possible so a repeat doesn't corrupt data
s4.validate: Errors are readable and suggest a fix, long lists are paginated, and the response structure is predictable.
s4.tip: A good error message saves a whole cycle: the model fixes the call itself instead of giving up. See [[node:m-debug|Debugging MCP]].

s5.title: Resources vs tools
s5.why: Not everything should be a tool. Resources are readable data at an address with no side effects; tools are actions with arguments. Confusing the two bloats the surface and throws the model off.
instructions: Take each server element and ask: is this an action with arguments or just data to read
Model static and reference data (documents, configs, lookups) as resources
Keep tools only for operations that do something or depend on input parameters
Don't turn reading a reference into a tool — that's an extra call and extra surface
Check that resources are addressable and predictable, while tools carry a real action
s5.validate: Reference and static data is modeled as resources, and tools remain only for actions.
s5.tip: Simple test: if an operation has no arguments or side effects and is just a read — it's almost certainly a resource, not a tool.

s6.title: Anti-patterns and a review checklist
s6.why: A final run through the checklist catches problems before they start tripping up Claude. Anti-patterns are easier to spot as a list than at design time.
instructions: Walk the anti-patterns: universal tool, technical names, silent errors, no pagination, everything-as-tool
Check each tool: a clear verb name, a description with side effects, a minimal schema
Check responses: predictable structure, readable errors, pagination for lists
Make sure read and write are split and reference data is moved to resources
Run real scenarios in Claude and watch whether the model picks tools without hints
s6.validate: The server passed the checklist, known anti-patterns are removed, and in a real dialog Claude picks tools correctly.
s6.tip: Run 5-10 typical requests and watch the tool choices — that's more honest than any code review. Surface security is in [[node:m-security|MCP security]].

m-debug.title: MCP debugging
m-debug.subtitle: Systematically find why an MCP server won't connect or its tools aren't visible
m-debug.whatItIs: A hands-on course on diagnosing MCP. It teaches you to check connection status via /mcp in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]], isolate a server with the MCP Inspector, recognize common failures (server won't start, tools not visible, timeouts, Windows specifics) and read server logs. It ends with a working "server won't connect" checklist.
m-debug.approach: We move from the observable to the cause: first look at what /mcp says, then isolate the server in the Inspector, then read stderr. Each step narrows the search so you never guess blindly.
outcomes: Read /mcp output and understand the state of each server
Isolate an MCP server in the Inspector independently of Claude
Recognize the 4 main classes of failure by their symptoms
Find the cause in server logs via stderr and DEBUG
Apply the "server won't connect" checklist and reach a green status

applyIn.title: New server not visible
applyIn.description: You connected an MCP server from [[node:m-custom|your own code]] or the registry, but Claude won't use it — you diagnose it in minutes.

applyIn.title: Tools gone after an edit
applyIn.description: You changed a config or a tool schema and Claude stopped seeing the tools. The Inspector shows whether the schema is valid.

applyIn.title: Server crashes under load
applyIn.description: Long requests hit a timeout or the server crashes — the stderr logs show the exact failing line.

pitfalls: Blaming Claude for "not using MCP" — in 90% of cases the cause is a faulty tool description or a server auth error
Not checking /mcp before debugging — you skip the fastest status check there is
Debugging straight in Claude instead of the Inspector — you mix two variables and can't tell where the failure is
Ignoring stderr — that's exactly where the server writes the real reason for the crash
On Windows, running a stdio server without accounting for paths and wrappers (cmd /c, absolute paths) — a frequent cause of "server won't start"

exercises.question: You ran /mcp and the server shows as failed. Where do you start — the Claude config or the server itself?
exercises.hint: Isolate the variable: run the server separately (Inspector or by hand) and read stderr — this separates a config problem from a server problem.

exercises.question: The server shows as connected in /mcp, but Claude never calls any tool. Where do you look for the cause?
exercises.hint: Check the tool descriptions in the Inspector: if a description is empty or unclear, the model doesn't know when to use them. See [[node:m-patterns|tool design patterns]].

exercises.question: A stdio server works locally but not on Windows. What do you check first?
exercises.hint: Paths and the launch command: Windows often needs a cmd /c wrapper and absolute paths to the interpreter/script.

s1.title: Where to start diagnosis: connection status
s1.why: Before changing any code or config, you need the fact: is the server connected at all? Connection status is the cheapest, fastest check and immediately splits the problem into "server didn't start" versus "server runs but Claude won't use it".
instructions: State the symptom in one sentence: "server failed", "tools not visible", "call returns an error".
Open [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] and run /mcp — this is your first source of truth about state.
Identify the class of problem: status (connected/failed) versus behavior (connected but tools not called).
Don't touch code until you've seen the status — otherwise you're fixing blind.
s1.validate: You can name the server's current status and place the problem in one of two classes: "won't connect" or "connects but isn't used".
s1.tip: Write down the symptom before debugging. Half of "disappearing" problems are different symptoms that got confused with each other.

s2.title: The /mcp command in Claude Code: what it shows
s2.why: /mcp is the built-in diagnostic screen. It shows the list of servers, their status, visible tools and connection errors. Understanding its output answers most "why isn't it working" questions without any external tooling.
instructions: Run /mcp in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] and read the list of servers by the names from your config.
For each server, look at the status: connected, connecting or failed.
Expand a server and check its tool list — an empty list means the [[node:mcp|MCP]] server connected but exposed no tools.
Read the error text next to failed — it often contains the cause outright (command not found, auth rejected).
Cross-check against your config: do the name, command and transport (stdio/HTTP) match?
s2.validate: You can see the server status, its tool list and the error text (if any), and can say at which stage the connection breaks.
s2.tip: If /mcp shows failed with no clear text, that's the signal to move to server logs (step 5), where stderr will have the details.

s3.title: MCP Inspector for local debugging
s3.why: The Inspector runs an MCP server in isolation, without Claude. This removes half the variables: you see what the server actually exposes over the protocol — the tool list, their schemas, and call responses. If the server works in the Inspector but not in Claude, the problem is in the Claude config, not the server.
instructions: Run the Inspector against your server using the same command and transport (stdio or HTTP) as in your config.
Verify the server starts and returns a tool list — this confirms the [[node:mcp|MCP]] protocol works.
Expand each tool's schema: name, description, parameters — this shows whether the tool is clear to the model.
Call a tool manually with test parameters and inspect the response — this validates real execution.
Compare behavior in the Inspector and in /mcp: a mismatch points to a problem in the Claude integration.
s3.validate: You ran the server in the Inspector, saw its tools and successfully called at least one — so the server itself is healthy.
s3.tip: The Inspector is your "second witness". Always isolate the server here before blaming the Claude config or the model.

s4.title: Common connection failures
s4.why: Most problems reduce to four classes. Recognizing the class from the symptom narrows the search for the cause instantly, so you don't try everything at random.
instructions: Server won't start: check the launch command, absolute paths and the presence of the interpreter — often the command simply isn't found.
Tools not visible: server connected but the list is empty — check tool registration and schema validity in the Inspector.
Timeouts: slow startup or slow tool response — raise the time limit or optimize the handler.
Windows specifics: a stdio server needs a cmd /c wrapper and absolute paths; relative paths and a direct call often fail.
Auth errors: for HTTP servers, check tokens and headers — an authorization refusal looks like a failed connection.
s4.validate: Given a symptom, you can name one of the failure classes (won't start / tools not visible / timeout / Windows / auth) and know where to check the cause.
s4.tip: On Windows, start with paths and the launch command — that's the number one cause for stdio servers.

s5.title: Reading server logs
s5.why: When /mcp and the Inspector show the server is failing, only the server itself knows the exact cause. It writes it to stderr. Without logs you guess; with logs you see the precise failing line.
instructions: Enable verbose output: set DEBUG (or an equivalent) in the server's env-var in the config.
Restart the server and capture its stderr — that's where errors go, not stdout (which carries the protocol).
Find the first error by time — later ones are often just consequences of the first.
Match the message to the failure class from step 4: "command not found", "port in use", "auth failed", "timeout".
After a fix, check the logs again — confirm the error is gone, not replaced by a new one.
s5.validate: You found the first real error in stderr and can state its cause in words, not as a guess.
s5.tip: Never write debug output to stdout on a stdio server — it mixes with the protocol and breaks the connection. Use stderr only.

s6.title: "Server won't connect" checklist + verification
s6.why: A checklist turns debugging from chaos into a repeatable procedure. Going through it top to bottom brings the server to a green status and tells you which item held the cause.
instructions: 1. /mcp in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]: is the status connected or failed?
2. Inspector: does the server start and expose tools in isolation?
3. Logs: what's in stderr — is there a first error and which class does it belong to?
4. Config: do the command, transport (stdio/HTTP), paths and env-vars match what works in the Inspector?
5. Environment: on Windows — cmd /c and absolute paths; for HTTP — tokens and headers.
s6.validate: After running the checklist, /mcp shows the server as connected, its tools are visible, and Claude successfully calls at least one tool.
s6.tip: Keep this checklist next to your project. The next "won't connect" you'll close in 5 minutes instead of an hour.
